188206a1-d745-4ad4-9fec-6da024cdd1da.body:
"The jacket of the sailor suit has a detachable collar and detachable cuffs, fastened with little buttons. That was of course very practical, because a light-coloured children's suit like this had to be washable.

But for the restoration, the cream wool and the dark blue cotton cuffs and collar could not be washed together. Wool and cotton react differently in water, and dark textiles can bleed onto light ones. The whole suit was dirty and grubby. Dirt speeds up the degradation of textiles, so I wanted to wash the suit. Just like in the old days, I took off the cuffs and collar and washed them separately."
188206a1-d745-4ad4-9fec-6da024cdd1da.title: Practical for the wash

2406baec-aa3b-475a-9ce1-8a7f1fbb8561.body:
“Two moths are living in my old coat
And those two moths have only just moved in
You're simply thrown when you see that young happiness
He's eating my whole coat to bits, just for her, that sweetie of a moth” 

"Dutch readers will probably recognise this song: in 1957 the damage moths can do to clothing inspired Tom Manders (cartoonist and comedian, 1921-1972), who wrote a whole song about it for his character Dorus.

It just goes to show: what annoys one person can be very inspiring for another."
2406baec-aa3b-475a-9ce1-8a7f1fbb8561.title: Inspiring moth holes

d4bcfe94-b4f7-4dce-a2c1-0f729c283fa3.body:
"Small round holes in your woollen clothes: who doesn't know them? They are traces of moths, and this sailor suit has several too.

Moths like to live in dark places and love wool. Adult moths don't eat wool, but they lay their eggs on clothing so their babies (larvae) can start eating straight away. So a wardrobe is paradise for them!

For a garment in a museum collection, a single small hole like this one is not a problem; we leave it as it is. Larger moth holes can seriously weaken the fabric, so the restorer supports them from the back.
d4bcfe94-b4f7-4dce-a2c1-0f729c283fa3.title: A tasty snack

dba802d4-3299-4d7f-ab52-92f2a2beb023.body:
"The sailor suit is one of the first examples of real children's clothing, which appeared at the end of the 19th century. These clothes gave children, both boys and girls, more freedom of movement. Boys wore it with socks and flat shoes or lace-up boots.

But before that, they had to be potty-trained. A good example can be seen in the photo of the sons of Arthur Klep and Willy Klep-van den Biesen. The Klep family founded the Royal Iron Foundries and Enamelling Works De Etna NV in Breda. The four sons of this family sit on one bench for the photo, and only the youngest has not yet won his sailor suit."
dba802d4-3299-4d7f-ab52-92f2a2beb023.title: Children as sailors

f68abb8c-84f2-47a5-82fa-72daeebffecc.body:
"The silk bow ribbons sewn onto the jacket of the sailor suit were in very poor condition. The silk was falling apart completely and parts were already lost. Still, I wanted to keep the ribbons.

Before the jacket was washed, the ribbons were taken off. To be able to treat them, they first had to be brought back into shape. I did this by moistening them very slightly with an ultrasonic humidifier. The moisture relaxes the fibres, after which the ribbons could be flattened under a glass plate.

Then the ribbons were fully supported with custom-cut strips of silk crepeline. After treatment the ribbons were sewn back onto the jacket to shine for the presentation."
f68abb8c-84f2-47a5-82fa-72daeebffecc.title: Fragile silk ribbons

416e0d1f-093b-cdde-aba5-76f90e208532.body:
"Apart from the wide silhouette, Jeanne Lanvin did not take much from the fashion of earlier centuries in her designs. The ornamentation is strongly simplified here, with a few parurerie flowers scattered at random as on a rose bush, and a repeating fan pattern along the hem. Just as in this design drawing by Lanvin.

This gives a very different picture from the lavishly decorated "lampshade" fashion of the Belle Époque, as Coco Chanel called it."
416e0d1f-093b-cdde-aba5-76f90e208532.title: Parurerie flowers

ec9452fa-a5ba-0552-389f-761d9ccae0fb.body: "When we see an emphasised waist flowing into a wide skirt, we don't immediately think of the tomboyish gowns of the 1920s. But the low waist and knee-length skirt give away its origin: we can see this gown as a model example of the robe de style. Jeanne Lanvin found a happy medium between the classic feminine silhouette and the revolutionary new style of the flappers."
ec9452fa-a5ba-0552-389f-761d9ccae0fb.title: The stylish middle way

41d2447c-3efc-48ab-ab5f-510eb8e59502.body:
"All sorts of embroidery techniques are on this piece. Green leaves or bands are made of interlacing stitch with a herringbone-type foundation. This is one of the characteristic filling stitches of Kutch domestic embroidery. A chain stitch is used to make the borders of the leaves and form flower petals.

Lastly, small glass discs are held in place by a framework of stitches and then enclosed in a ring of stitching; this is the Shisha technique. The uneven surface is typical of older mirror glass, which was blown into large bubbles, silvered on the inside and cut into small pieces. Some mirrors are missing, either lost or were never applied to the cloth."
41d2447c-3efc-48ab-ab5f-510eb8e59502.title: A myriad of hand embroidery techniques

9bccaf31-0d31-4234-810c-ba85723c82c9.body: "This hood was clearly worn and cared for. On the inside, a small patch covers a hole, and the mending fabric itself shows another of India's best-known textile techniques: bandhani, or tie-dye. Before dyeing, small points of the cloth are pinched up and tightly bound with thread. The bound areas resist the dye, leaving the pattern of tiny rings and dots typical of bandhani."
9bccaf31-0d31-4234-810c-ba85723c82c9.title: Mending as a sign of care

2cb7e1d0-8d8b-4b16-b409-c1275dd0699f.body: "This coat from Yamuna's Sisterhood not CISterhood collection consists of five parts: front, back, two sleeves and a collar. Yamuna sewed the coat together by hand and decorated it with pearls to give it an even more precious look."
2cb7e1d0-8d8b-4b16-b409-c1275dd0699f.title: Diamonds are a sister's best friend

65671bd5-123a-472b-b3f2-84e481153bd8.body:
"Can you see the different lines in Yamuna's design?

With the circular knitting machine at the TextielMuseum, two separate layers can be knitted at once with a lining in between, creating a kind of quilted fabric."
65671bd5-123a-472b-b3f2-84e481153bd8.title: Double cloth, a.k.a. quilt

9390a0e1-d53a-4a11-820e-a4c5eefb5e27.body:
"Thanks to the many needles in the circular knitting machine, it is very precise and can make very detailed images. The technique is therefore also well suited to knitting letters, and Yamuna took that chance.

In her project, typography and proudly using her own name as a brand play an important role. She wanted to question the unwritten rules of the fashion world, not only around gender but also the idea that only world-famous brands can use their name as a design."
9390a0e1-d53a-4a11-820e-a4c5eefb5e27.title: Typography in textile

c084d6b7-6e1a-44ce-8ec9-c494316b42f4.body:
"In 2018 Yamuna created the Sisterhood not CIsterhood collection, for which several fabrics were knitted at the TextielLab. For this, the circular knitting machine was used, which can knit with 1680 needles and six colours at once. 

A project like this calls for special expertise, because the digital design has to be translated into the machine's software. In the professional workshop of the TextielMuseum she worked closely with product developer and knitting specialist Mathilde Vandenbussche to bring the very detailed design to life."
c084d6b7-6e1a-44ce-8ec9-c494316b42f4.title: Knitted with 1680 needles

8f3ec23e-05e4-4112-a8d5-d7be078b862b.body: "If you look inside through the sleeves, you can see the pencil lines Alet Pilon drew before folding the fabric in these places. This makes you more aware of the mathematical insight behind the design."
8f3ec23e-05e4-4112-a8d5-d7be078b862b.title: A visible design process

c9ca3de7-f151-46da-bfd9-ddf107cb564a.body: "At first sight the piece looks a bit like a bolero or a short jacket, but it turns out to be completely closed at the front and has to be pulled on over the head. Although the two circular parts form an elegant neckline by themselves, the rest of the architectural shape, made of stiffened canvas, completely hides any body shapes underneath."
c9ca3de7-f151-46da-bfd9-ddf107cb564a.title: A jacket that stands like a house

5e63bb2d-9170-48a1-880e-ddec474f4a58.body:
"This necklace dazzles you. But it is not real diamonds or gold! Iradj Moini makes so-called ‘costume jewellery’, or fashion jewellery. This type of jewellery almost never consists of precious metals or other expensive materials, which does not necessarily mean it is not valuable or precious.

Costume jewellery has been produced on a small scale since the eighteenth century, but only really grew in popularity from the early twentieth century. This was due to increasing industrialisation, new production methods and the rise of fashion designers who began using jewellery widely in their collections, such as Coco Chanel and Elsa Schiaparelli."
5e63bb2d-9170-48a1-880e-ddec474f4a58.title: All that glitters is not gold..

b1994267-8239-489c-886c-a5fccd06755c.body: "Iradj Moini's jewellery became even better known because the American style icon Iris Apfel (1921-2024) loved wearing it. Apfel died in 2024 at the age of 102 and was known for her flamboyant style, combining flea-market jewellery with designer pieces. She loved wearing costume jewellery, and lots of it, preferably all at once! This necklace is a perfect example of her over-the-top style; her motto was ‘more is more’. Would you dare to wear this necklace?"
b1994267-8239-489c-886c-a5fccd06755c.title: More is more!

e137a2eb-a2bb-4236-887e-8f2ecddf6f92.body: "When Iradj Moini went to the United States to escape the situation in his home country of Iran, he first studied architecture. I think you can still see this clearly in the way he builds up large pieces like this. From the side you can see how three-dimensional this necklace is, and that the structure is built up from several layers. A bit like how, behind the facade of a building, beams and bricks are needed to keep everything standing!"
e137a2eb-a2bb-4236-887e-8f2ecddf6f92.title: Wearable architecture

16e34cd8-2e4b-4c67-abef-61c828ccdd78.body:
"For church, people in West Brabant wore a 'tight cap', and on special occasions a pleated lace cap like this one.

This 'pleated cap' was put on over the black under-cap and consists of a crown of embroidered tulle and pleated front strips of bobbin lace. Finally, a richly decorated 'crown' goes over the 'double cap'. This is a separate band stiffened with gauze, with small white artificial flowers and a ribbon with woven floral patterns. At the back of the head, the ribbon is closed with hooks and eyes."
16e34cd8-2e4b-4c67-abef-61c828ccdd78.title: Ribbon over the pleated cap

1eb7de83-def7-4a80-9af9-c2be560d36eb.body:
"Around 1900 a simple cap was worn in Brabant on working days, but on Sundays and holidays people went all out. In western Brabant, the barony of Breda and the Marquisate, women wore a floral headdress on their cap: the crown, also called the kroezel.

The crown is a cloud of tulle and small fabric flowers on a silk ribbon. As the icing on the cake, the wearer could also order "dew drops" from the cap maker. These glass drops were set between the flowers on little iron wires. They sparkle in the sunlight, and depending on your budget you could have up to a hundred of them put in your crown."
1eb7de83-def7-4a80-9af9-c2be560d36eb.title: A sparkle in the sea of flowers

23738c3e-6738-4af5-a723-ecfea9f571c5.body:
"In 1956 Kee van Eekelen-de Kock from De Kladde, in West Brabant dress, demonstrated step by step for the Netherlands Open Air Museum in Arnhem how the cap was put on.

First the hair is pinned up in a bun quite high on the back of the head. Then a black band with two small strands of false hair, sewn on in the middle, is placed around the forehead and tied. The strands of hair are laid in two equal little arches on the forehead, so that they will show just under the front edge of the cap. These strands of hair are called 'blesjes'. Then a black under-cap is put on and fastened around the head with ties. The under-cap protects the white cap from grease in the hair."
23738c3e-6738-4af5-a723-ecfea9f571c5.title: Blesjes under the cap

59d501e4-f55b-40bc-9b14-0bf4344eb47f.body:
"Where a bride today wears a tiara or a veil, a Brabant woman around 1900 wore her lace cap and crown. Together with a fashionable gown of black silk , this was the usual bridal outfit.

In this photo we see Pieter Johannis Crassaarts (cattle dealer) and Adriana Cornelia van Overveld (no profession) on their wedding day, 31 October 1901 in Steenbergen. He was 35 and she 34 when they married. Adriana wore the gown for a long time after her wedding as her Sunday best; we can tell from all the alterations made to it."
59d501e4-f55b-40bc-9b14-0bf4344eb47f.title: Queen for a day

56da77dd-97d5-474c-a28f-d703af0cef59.body:
"Can you see from this little dress why it signals half mourning? The court dress code for mourning made clear to the outside world that people were in mourning, and how deeply: over time it went from full mourning to half mourning to light mourning. King William III died in 1890, when Queen Wilhelmina was ten years old. Full mourning was declared at court immediately after his death.

Only after 39 weeks was full court mourning replaced by half mourning, which after ten weeks became light mourning for three weeks. Although Queen Dowager Emma followed the prescribed court rules for mourning strictly, they were relaxed for the young queen. Next to her mother's all-black appearance (by then she also wore a cap with a mourning veil), Wilhelmina already appeared in a half-mourning dress with a combination of black and white details."
56da77dd-97d5-474c-a28f-d703af0cef59.title: Court etiquette for mourning

80bb1704-3a90-4f0a-af09-9ae73242124b.body:
"Mourning clothes expressed grief and mood. After the death of William III, Queen Regent Emma wanted to make the monarchy visible again, among other things through photography, in which the young little queen in mourning made a powerful image.

With its leg-of-mutton sleeves, the girl's dress followed the fashion of grown women. With the dress, Wilhelmina wore black stockings, black shoes and a loose black belt around the waist. The large white hats she wore with it were decorated with black details, such as ostrich feathers dyed black. During her annual visit to the capital in 1891, the first without the king, Wilhelmina wore, according to De Avondpost of 28 May, ‘a little white gown with black embroidery and a white hat with long feathers’. This etching shows Wilhelmina in a similar half-mourning dress."
80bb1704-3a90-4f0a-af09-9ae73242124b.title: Portrait in mourning

263006bf-e3f8-42ac-a33c-48469743d8b4.body: "Jewellery maker Vera Siemund is often inspired by historical motifs. The two ‘bells’ hanging from this necklace are inspired by the shapes of Biedermeier skirts. The Biedermeier period ran from about 1815 to 1848 and was found mainly in Germany and Austria. After a long period of war, people longed for cosiness, friendly shapes and domestic life. The style was romantic and feminine, with lots of ruffles, pleats and floral motifs on clothing. Can you find that in this piece of jewellery?"
263006bf-e3f8-42ac-a33c-48469743d8b4.title: Skirt day

4b1b797a-23a9-4b88-aeab-6cb9362ca543.body:
"Vera Siemund's work often refers to classical ornaments from history and architecture. The ornaments are mainly made of iron, copper and enamel, but she does not shy away from silver, gold and gemstones. She saws all her elements by hand, down to the smallest details.

At the centre of this necklace are two hanging ornaments made of enamel with a flower and leaf motif and scalloped edges, inspired by shapes from the Biedermeier period. The ornaments hang from a string of gold links with glass beads between them."
4b1b797a-23a9-4b88-aeab-6cb9362ca543.title: Architectural shapes

74a4c338-f03e-4d07-9005-b07b12b22a7b.body: "The description of this piece says it was made as bridal jewellery. What could tell you that? I immediately thought of the bells often rung in church at traditional weddings. At the bottom of the porcelain ‘skirts’ hang a kind of little clappers, which make a soft sound when they touch the porcelain. I imagine a traditional Austrian wedding, perhaps with people in folk costume. Traditions around brides differ from culture to culture. What do you associate with jewellery you would wear at a wedding?"
74a4c338-f03e-4d07-9005-b07b12b22a7b.title: Wedding Bells

1ed09ce1-0c16-27c3-9fa4-ad77b1b8ac5a.body: "Did you know this necklace is based on the style period we call Rococo? You may recognise the typical sweet pastel colours from the porcelain figurines produced by the German firm Meissen in the early eighteenth century. The Rococo period was all about elegance, lightness and frivolity. Much of the porcelain from that time shows lovely, almost sugary scenes in which everything seems young and carefree, a kind of eternal spring in which decay and death do not exist. Think also of the paintings of French painters in particular, such as Fragonard, Boucher and Watteau."
1ed09ce1-0c16-27c3-9fa4-ad77b1b8ac5a.title: Rococo in porcelain

35f16835-0050-4967-a91c-fc547bd2b0fd.body: "The porcelain twigs and flowers you see here look as if they were modelled in clay, but they were made with moulds of real branches, which were then cast in porcelain! The ends of the branches have been broken off. The flowers on the necklace were originally real flowers dipped in porcelain and then attached to the branches. When the porcelain was fired in the kiln, the real flowers burned away, leaving only the porcelain."
35f16835-0050-4967-a91c-fc547bd2b0fd.title: Real flowers

22ac7982-af03-4a47-a2a1-a809a055796b.body:
"Simon van Gijn was a wealthy merchant, banker and lawyer. He became known above all for the extensive collections he built up during his life. Simon was born in Vlaardingen in 1836, the son of Cornelia Johanna Hooghwinkel and Dirk de Kater van Gijn. In 1842 the family moved to Dordrecht, where his father went to work at his father-in-law's banking firm. From a young age Simon developed a great interest in history. Encouraged by his mother, he began collecting historical prints. Art and the applied arts also interested him greatly.

Simon van Gijn invested the fortune he earned in his collections. He brought together an impressive collection of historical prints, weapons, ship models, coins, silver and ceramics. His most important collection is the Atlas Van Gijn, a print collection of more than 30,000 prints. His strong bond with Dordrecht and the city's history showed in his many historical and cultural activities. Besides being a collector, Van Gijn was also creative: he designed costumes for various occasions and was a gifted watercolourist and draughtsman.

His name lives on in the museum that bears it. Formerly 'Museum Mr Simon van Gijn', now 'Huis Van Gijn', in his former home at Nieuwe Haven 29 in Dordrecht."
22ac7982-af03-4a47-a2a1-a809a055796b.title: Simon van Gijn: a legacy

ef21af61-03db-4791-968f-6b88c668db77.body:
"Thanks to the account book (financial record) of Cornelia Hooghwinkel, Simon van Gijn's mother, we know exactly what Simon's masquerade costume cost. From 1844 to 1866 Cornelia kept careful track of what she spent on clothing for her family. In 1860, under the heading For the Masquerade June 1860 , she noted the following expenses:

f 68 the suit

f 9 the cap with feather

f 13 the boots

f 23 the sword

f 15 collars, gloves, etc

f128 in total, a hefty expense when you consider that this was about half of the yearly spending on Simon's clothes."
ef21af61-03db-4791-968f-6b88c668db77.title: The account book reveals

f92a73cd-2c90-4151-a81d-df11f29a5ac8.body:
"The Dutch student masquerades were unique in Europe in their size and organisation. Between 1814 and 1914 the student masquerade became a fixed tradition in the university cities of Groningen, Utrecht, Leiden and Delft. The masquerades, organised every five years as part of the university's lustrum celebration, were not only a cultural-historical phenomenon but also a performance and a ritual.

The grand Leiden masquerade of 1835 marked the shift from classical, oriental and burlesque themes to historical themes. Under the influence of Romanticism, the age of historical masquerades had begun, and it would last until 1914."
f92a73cd-2c90-4151-a81d-df11f29a5ac8.title: The romance of student masquerades

fd470d70-9642-4a7c-9cea-1e0448978fd3.body:
"Masquerade committees started work more than a year in advance, studying old chronicles, archives and costume books. The wish to be as authentic as possible reflected a romantic view of the past. In 1859 Simon van Gijn was appointed treasurer of the Leiden masquerade committee. In that role he was responsible for managing the finances and designing the costumes and accessories for the historical parade. He also designed his own costume.

As a committee member he received a gold signet ring with the coat of arms of the Leiden student society and the engraved date 11 June 1860."
fd470d70-9642-4a7c-9cea-1e0448978fd3.title: Costume design

418af3ee-6a81-4ff0-bb2c-f6534268073d.body:
"If you look closely at the circles on this silk kimono, the edges are never quite sharp. That blurred manner is deliberate. It recalls kasuri, the Japanese form of ikat, in which threads are bound and dyed before weaving.

But this kimono is made of meisen, a silk fabric that became fashionable in the early twentieth century. Many meisen makers skipped the slow binding process of Kasuri and instead printed the pattern onto the threads with stencils. The blurred edges stayed, and the shortcut allowed for bold designs like this one to be affordable for many more women."
418af3ee-6a81-4ff0-bb2c-f6534268073d.title: Blurry Circles

0bf9d795-e63f-434b-9a66-9b21368f3c14.body:
"Jan-Jan Van Essche is a designer from Antwerp. His aesthetic is marked by an interest in intercultural relationships and a love of craft. In his designs, Van Essche tries to leave as much freedom as possible to the wearer, giving you the chance to shape the garment yourself.

Van Essche only uses materials of natural origin and has a preference for natural dyeing processes. He also values intercultural collaborations with workshops and craftspeople. The shoes with this silhouette, for example, are the result of an ongoing collaboration with a Japanese shoe workshop, and the hat was developed with an Austrian hat company with a long tradition."
0bf9d795-e63f-434b-9a66-9b21368f3c14.title: Intercultural collaborations

4a962fba-ce3c-4fde-838d-6c150e416288.body:
"Lamine Diouf is a Belgian-Senegalese textile artist who has worked closely with Antwerp fashion designer Jan-Jan Van Essche for years. For each collection they design and develop a handwoven textile as material for garments and accessories.

In this silhouette we see robe#1, a kind of poncho made of two rectangular panels, finished with fringes at the short sides. The panels are handwoven from cotton, linen and wool yarns from Van Essche's archive. Lamine develops the pattern and the weave structure. The pieces are assembled by hand by the team in Van Essche's studio, as you can see from the hand stitches in contrasting thread."
4a962fba-ce3c-4fde-838d-6c150e416288.title: Handwoven panels

632959b3-25fd-4e8a-997d-23b69c004422.body:
"With his designs, Jan-Jan Van Essche wants to give the wearer as much freedom of movement as possible. For him it is important that the body shapes the garment and not the other way round. This translates into a rather simple, pared-back cut, reminiscent of Japanese kimonos or African boubous, for example. Pattern drafting is an important part of Van Essche's design process, and he is actively involved in it himself. 

Thanks to this focus on freedom of movement, Van Essche has also worked with choreographers several times, including Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui."
632959b3-25fd-4e8a-997d-23b69c004422.title: Patterns for free movement

b01286f5-6a32-401b-bb8b-33b0af4de54c.body:
“In the eighteenth century, well-to-do women and their daughters had stays made to measure. This was done by a master staymaker, a specialised tailor. Stays are a bodice fully fitted with whalebone. They close with a lace at the back, so women and girls needed help putting them on and taking them off. These stays were usually spiral-laced.

The stays gave the wearer's upper body a straight, conical shape. They also formed the basis (literally: foundation) of the outer clothing; the gown was worn smoothly over the stays. Even young girls were fitted with stays at an early age, and this object is an example."
b01286f5-6a32-401b-bb8b-33b0af4de54c.title: Lacing

d3052ccc-d7bd-41fe-a7a2-43e15eb939bc.body: "In the last quarter of the eighteenth century, several booklets appeared arguing against wearing stays. The French Revolution brought a new fashion with a slender silhouette, without stays and hooped skirts (paniers). In the nineteenth century, stays were replaced by corsets, which often only had a wide, stiff busk at the centre front and little or no other boning. This new fashion was a real relief compared with the eighteenth century.”
d3052ccc-d7bd-41fe-a7a2-43e15eb939bc.title: Whalebone

1070886a-d660-438b-b7df-335d80fd70cb.body:
"Can you see this seam here? The fabric of the coat was machine-embroidered in advance, without taking the future wearer into account. It was then the tailor's job to place the embroidery so that it ended up in the right places on the body.

The length of the embroidery on the front was fixed. To adjust it to the wearer's height, in this case a small seam was added at the shoulder of the front panel.

In another coat in the Rijksmuseum collection, a different solution was chosen: there the seam was placed at pocket height, where it subtly disappears into the embroidery around the pocket opening."
1070886a-d660-438b-b7df-335d80fd70cb.title: A seam as the solution

1b176e41-a0c5-4474-9896-24675eb26901.body:
How did the Habit à la Française get this characteristic shape?

When the three-piece men's suit came into fashion in the Baroque period around 1680, the fronts of the waistcoat and coat were still straight, so they could be closed completely.

As the 18th century went on, the closure became more and more minimal. The coat closed with fewer and fewer buttons, and sometimes the buttons were only decorative. The coat fronts then closed with hooks and eyes at chest height.

On this coat, the fronts are cut away so far that they can no longer be closed at all. This gives the embroidered waistcoat underneath a new, more prominent role."
1b176e41-a0c5-4474-9896-24675eb26901.title: A cut-away front

aa382b0f-7a0b-643b-c96f-0e028f737542.body:
"This Habit à la Française from the collection is a kind of compilation of garments that did not originally belong together. There are two possible explanations. Either this compilation is the work of the auction house where we bought the ensemble in 2006, or it goes back to the 18th century, when the pieces were made. At that time there was a lively trade in second-hand clothing.

Because fabrics were so expensive, garments were often passed down for generations, resulting in ensembles made up of different pieces that did not originally belong together. 'Patchwork' outfits like this one, at the Modemuseum Hasselt and in many other museums, are therefore quite historically accurate."
aa382b0f-7a0b-643b-c96f-0e028f737542.title: A 'patchwork' outfit

be572174-faea-96ae-e4dc-40ae4e14afb9.body:
"Mounting a Habit à la Française from around 1770-1790 turned out to be unexpectedly complex. A historical ensemble is often put together from different parts that were once worn by different bodies, because in the time of this habit clothes were only made to measure. The breeches, waistcoat and coat differed too much from standard sizes to be mounted on an ordinary mannequin.

When we mounted the habit on a mannequin with legs and arms, however, a different body, and so a different life, appeared. Although the separate pieces did not match in size, they did roughly match the body of a young adult, a teenager."
be572174-faea-96ae-e4dc-40ae4e14afb9.title: A growth spurt or a pieced-together outfit?

c26da832-62a6-44ac-bb78-dd81fadb51a8.body:
"The fit of this coat is very different from what we are used to today. The back is strikingly narrow and the armhole runs far towards the back. As soon as the wearer puts on the coat, his shoulders are automatically pulled back, so the chest comes forward: the male ideal of beauty at the time.

In earlier fashion trends the body had to fit an ideal, while today we work towards the body. The body to be clothed has become the starting point."
c26da832-62a6-44ac-bb78-dd81fadb51a8.title: Shape determines posture

c4253445-45b1-4d40-9aac-adfe7a82b8bc.body:
"The fabrics for the waistcoat and coat were machine-embroidered in advance, without taking the size of the future wearer into account.

The front, around the pocket opening and the vent, but also parts such as the collar, pocket flaps, cuffs and even the buttons were already laid out and embroidered on the fabric. The placement of the embroidery was therefore important for whoever had to make the clothes to measure ."
c4253445-45b1-4d40-9aac-adfe7a82b8bc.title: Embroidered in advance

59048e2b-99a5-03c6-5a5e-f9d0211fda8b.body:
"In 1969 Nicolaas van Beek took part in an exhibition at the Van Abbe Museum, ‘Objects to Wear’. It also showed work by Emmy van Leersum, Gijs Bakker, Françoise van den Bosch and Bernhard Laméris. The exhibition set out to show that among a number of jewellery makers there was a visible shift from jewellery as ornament, used mainly as a finishing touch on clothing, to an independent object that happens to be wearable as well.

Jewellery was now truly seen as an autonomous object. The design behind it and the material research that went with it were more important than ever."
59048e2b-99a5-03c6-5a5e-f9d0211fda8b.title: Jewellery: ornament or object?

5fc169ff-38ac-fa95-a32c-c8d776ce6572.body: "It is quite remarkable that you can make such an organic shape from a sheet of stainless steel. Nicolaas van Beek originally trained as a sculptor, and the sculptural has always been the dominant note in his work. He thought exploring shapes was very important and experimented a lot with bending, sawing and deforming sheets of metal, as you can see very clearly in this head ornament."
5fc169ff-38ac-fa95-a32c-c8d776ce6572.title: Bending, sawing, turning?

916b903b-489c-b0f9-e289-f629749b2c10.body: "What does this head ornament remind you of? Despite its modern look, I immediately thought of an oorijzer (ear iron), the special ornament worn as part of traditional dress in some Dutch regions. Originally the ear iron was a metal band that held caps in place. Over time it grew into a real showpiece, like the wide gold ear irons made in Friesland."
916b903b-489c-b0f9-e289-f629749b2c10.title: Diadem, space helmet or ear iron?

b8e9898f-c261-a6c5-660b-ec99dfb45502.body:
"Space Age fashion from the 1960s was inspired by the space race and technological progress. Designers such as Courrèges and Cardin gave fashion an innovative character through futuristic shapes, geometric lines and new materials. Space Age fashion is the outfit you wear for your first meeting with aliens.

The futuristic jewellery of Nicolaas van Beek, inspired by spatial forms and modern materials, carries the same forward-looking spirit as Space Age fashion."
b8e9898f-c261-a6c5-660b-ec99dfb45502.title: Fashion for space travel

05f50f27-ddcb-4106-90be-eeff2160e912.body: "The rectangles and squares that make up the object are tied together with a twisted, painted ribbon. The ribbon has a long loose end that ends in a small bobbin. Several of Lam de Wolf's objects have an element like this, each with a different ‘pendant’ at the end, such as a little ball or a satay skewer: her unique ‘label’."
05f50f27-ddcb-4106-90be-eeff2160e912.title: Lam de Wolf's signature

463fd631-3904-4a6a-8ce2-0fc1c1ebc541.body: "The wearable object is built from rectangles, tied together at the short sides with a cord. The object is put together very simply, but at the same time it is very versatile: it can be worn around the neck like a traditional necklace, hung on the wall as a wall piece, or set down as a sculpture."
463fd631-3904-4a6a-8ce2-0fc1c1ebc541.title: Simple construction, many uses

803d020b-48dd-4195-9523-ab75d1eac5e6.body: "The piece of jewellery is built from wooden sticks in rectangular and square shapes, wrapped in painted strips of fabric and held together with a cord. The linear shape refers to a textile element: the thread."
803d020b-48dd-4195-9523-ab75d1eac5e6.title: Thread as inspiration

56d171a3-73b2-4847-9ac5-83c216aaa340.body:
Jef Montes: “As a fashion designer I use textiles as the basis for my dress patterns. When I use the patterns to get a fitted effect, leftover material is created: waste! This is an unsustainable process and harmful to nature. During weaving it is possible to produce rectangular patterns, but dress patterns have curves to bring out the shape of the female body. So I came up with the idea of starting from a rectangular pattern and building those curves into the fabric itself. Shaping a woven fabric in 3D, but the question was: how?

Together with the Aitex Textile Institute in Alcoy I developed the Adaptive Archi-Filament, a yarn that can transform from a flat shape into a 3D shape. The goal of my project Marinero was to let nature ‘shape’ a garment, so that nature and the design process melt into one, as it were. This way we could use the rectangular piece made at the TextielMuseum as the base pattern, and the Adaptive Archi-Filament shaped the dress in the rain. The balance of techniques in design 33 made sure the process in the rain transformed it into a fitted shape, purely through the shaping of the yarns, so without any leftover material or other production processes that harm nature.”
56d171a3-73b2-4847-9ac5-83c216aaa340.title: A waste without waste

8c52ec39-df10-4cf8-b1d1-6965b9374691.body:
"The dress consists of a rectangular piece of woven fabric folded in half across its width and sewn closed at the sides. In the middle of the rectangle the fabric has no weft threads: here we only see the transparent monofilament warp threads (the vertical threads) without weft threads (the horizontal threads).

In the dress, this part forms the neck, shoulders and sleeves. If you zoom in further on the fabric, you can see that the weft threads form wide bands and hang a little loose because they are not woven tightly. These are called floats. When exposed to the weather, these threads shrink, which changes the shape of the dress."
8c52ec39-df10-4cf8-b1d1-6965b9374691.title: Complex fabric, simple construction

935a9f12-f123-4016-a014-c545952f1935.body:
"In his project ‘Marinero’, Jef Montes worked with various knowledge partners in Europe to develop yarns that react strongly to their surroundings: Adaptive Archi-filament. This yarn has a coating that melts in water, after which the yarn reacts by curling strongly. This gives it a three-dimensional effect.

Montes used this yarn in woven and knitted garments. He then placed them outside, so that the weather gave them their often surprising final shape. Here we see a jacquard-woven dress from this collection after it was placed outside. The weather has shaped the design."
935a9f12-f123-4016-a014-c545952f1935.title: Before & After

1bddded9-83bf-9a9d-dac0-bd60600b3e1a.body:
"Colourful embroidered tropical plants and amphibians catch our eye on this overall. The meaning behind the scene is less idyllic. The appliquéd bones on the sleeves and trouser legs hold up a mirror to us: if we do not treat our planet more sustainably, humanity is digging its own grave. 

A topical message that Van Beirendonck already delivered in 2006 with this collection, 'Stop Terrorizing our World'. In particular he raises the clear-cutting of the Amazon rainforest, and criticises unbridled neoliberalism. The portrait of pop icon Madonna, embroidered on the separate hoodie, stands for the greed of the West."
1bddded9-83bf-9a9d-dac0-bd60600b3e1a.title: Colourful embroidery as hidden social criticism

e830ae08-9798-7c47-a7d1-6defadf33817.body:
"What connects tradition and fashion? Walter Van Beirendonck answers with a hoodie with a wide trim of faux fur, referring to the traditional dress of peoples around the Arctic Circle.

With it he draws attention to the threatened way of life of people and animals in the Arctic, caused by the capitalist exploitation of the region's natural resources and increasing global warming."
e830ae08-9798-7c47-a7d1-6defadf33817.title: An Arctic reference

3dee65f8-5f42-4a53-ab32-b7bc5beaef27.body: "Is papier-mâché the first material you would think of for a goldsmith? People still often think of silver or gold when it comes to jewellery. But when Marion Herbst started making jewellery, she wanted to use completely different materials, such as perspex and later a lot of textiles. This gave her great freedom to focus much more on form and colour. At the end of the sixties, jewellery was very sleek and smooth, like the modern jewellery of Gijs Bakker and Emmy van Leersum. Marion Herbst did things completely differently and used exactly the materials she felt like using!"
3dee65f8-5f42-4a53-ab32-b7bc5beaef27.title: The new gold?

3fddf185-531c-4cde-9483-9ae9ef27a91d.body: "Marion Herbst was one of the founders of the BOE group: the Bond van Oproerige Edelsmeden (League of Rebellious Goldsmiths)! Together with Francoise van den Bosch, Karel Niehorster, Onno Boekhoudt and Berend Peter, the group wanted to rebel against the prevailing norms of the jewellery world. An important point for the group was that they wanted jewellery to be seen as a real art object , and they also found it important to show the process. So they made the ‘BOE box’, in which you saw not only the end product but also the path to it. That is why we present this object as art too, hanging on a stand instead of worn around a neck."
3fddf185-531c-4cde-9483-9ae9ef27a91d.title: The BOE group

bbf4f8b9-f655-40b5-8fe6-dfbec4920ca3.body:
"Can you see where the red, white and blue of the Dutch flag is hidden in the necklace? With it, Marion Herbst celebrates Dutch pride with the iconic colours.

Colour plays an important role in her work. In 1978 she already made the series ‘lintjes’ (ribbons). She was inspired by the often cheerful decorations that come out of the cupboard on special occasions, but also put off by the strict way they have to be pinned on according to rules and tradition. By using them in her work, she tries to take away this symbolism."
bbf4f8b9-f655-40b5-8fe6-dfbec4920ca3.title: Orange on top!

5be89d0f-5466-2f87-76ce-f7f5f6944fc6.body:
"The uniform was designed by commander Louis de Becdelièvre, who described it as “halfway between the uniform of the Zouaves of Africa and that of the French infantryman” 

Commander Becdelièvre did meet some resistance at the Papal Ministry of War when trying to get his design made: “The gentlemen of this department did not understand the advantages of the muted grey camouflage colour of this, already very modern, uniform. [..] The commander, kept on a short leash, then asked for a personal audience with Pius IX. The Pope was immediately won over by this new dress and praised its looseness and ease. And so this uniform was introduced at the proposal of the Pope."

Written by Amanda Elshout
5be89d0f-5466-2f87-76ce-f7f5f6944fc6.title: How a uniform came about

728ff6dc-0e56-70ac-26c8-2c9303c4d8b5.body:
"This uniform belonged to a soldier; an officer's uniform was more richly decorated. The attached photo shows that the officer had black instead of red chevrons and gold thread as distinguishing features. This way of decorating with passementerie later shows up in fashion too, for example on the cape in the collection of the Amsterdam Museum.

It is remarkable that this jacket has survived: no Dutch boys made it to officer. But thanks to Brother Christofoor, who worked to preserve the Zouaves' heritage, this one ended up in the collection of the Bisschoppelijk Museum."
728ff6dc-0e56-70ac-26c8-2c9303c4d8b5.title: Fashionable soldiers and officers

eaead830-7fd1-4b3a-811e-4aeaac5cadd2.body:
"For the ordinary Roman Catholic man in the street, going to Italy to fight in the Pope's army was a boyhood dream. Cornelis Mermans from Breda signed up, and on 22 December 1866 he entered service as a papal Zouave. In the photo we see him posing in his uniform with a kepi (cap).

He took part in the Battle of Mentana on 2 November 1867, and in the last four months of his service he worked as a ‘sapper’, digging trenches. After returning to Breda in early 1869, Cornelis became a bricklayer and married Cornelia Antoinetta Clarijs."
eaead830-7fd1-4b3a-811e-4aeaac5cadd2.title: Cornelis with the kepi

f687bfd7-68bc-4b14-8e7f-8f93b7478a2e.body:
"The Zouave's uniform was used intensively. This is especially visible on the trousers. On the knees you can see wear in the red piping. The detail photo shows that the waistband has been mended with different patches of fabric, sewn on with rough stitches. Maybe Cornelis Mermans, who wore this uniform, did the repairs himself!

The uniform is made of thick, heavy wool. The whole weight of the trousers hangs from the waistband, and the waistband was also pulled on when dressing and undressing. No wonder the waistband suffered most."
f687bfd7-68bc-4b14-8e7f-8f93b7478a2e.title: A visible history of use

41cfbe8e-cb53-41a0-8118-ad1292662219.body:
"Each ethic group inside Afghanistan has its own specific way of living and culture, which is often reflected in their traditional embroidery. Embroidery is used to decorate a wide range of objects and the clothing of both men and women. Women’s clothing tends to be more elaborately and colourfully embroidered than that of men.

Beads and large mirrors are often used in Pashtun women’s dresses, while beads, coins and shells are often found on the dresses worn by nomadic women. Pashtun and Baluchi women also include small mirrors (shisha) in their works; an idea that originates.

The Pashtun constitute an ethnic group that lives along both sides of the modern Afghanistan-Pakistan border (the still disputed so-called Durand line of 1896)."
41cfbe8e-cb53-41a0-8118-ad1292662219.title: Eye-catching embroidery

e0a1ed5a-41e4-4bad-bfb9-45b3e9305873.body:
"We have become so used to white wedding dresses, we forget other cultures celebrate various colours. Afghan brides traditionally wear red or green clothing (colours with symbolic and religious significance), although some modern brides wear white dresses based on Western fashions.

Usually, a red gown will have gold decorative features, while a green one like this one may feature silver embroidery. The colour of the decorative braid along the hem of the bride's trousers corresponds to the braids on the dress and the head covering. Brides and grooms often change clothing several times during the wedding day, and a white Western gown for the bride is easily swapped for a traditional ethnic outfit later in the day."
e0a1ed5a-41e4-4bad-bfb9-45b3e9305873.title: Colours of a wedding

53a9d9a4-7be6-448a-993f-0d4c7b8b8133.body:
"In the play “Uit liefde voor de kunst” (For the love of art), Queen Wilhelmina played the role of the countess, a fashionable Parisian woman who, by her own account, had put her wardrobe together with care. Queen Wilhelmina's costume emphasises this theme: the gored skirt, full shoulders and high neckline of the gown are typical of the prevailing silhouette of the 1890s.

The hat looks contemporary too, with its emphasis on vertical lines and lavishly arranged flowers and ribbons. The play, performed on 2 August 1897 for the 39th birthday of her mother Queen Emma in the theatre at Het Loo Palace, takes place in a salon: Wilhelmina may be wearing the hat indoors because, according to the story, the countess is on her way out."
53a9d9a4-7be6-448a-993f-0d4c7b8b8133.title: Clothes make the countess

d8e61402-b4e8-4c50-ba21-d804e5cdeb82.body: "The decoration on this bonnet is made of bleached and braided horsehair. Extremely strong and easy to get, it was a popular material for decorating the regional dress of Zeeland and Brabant. Here it is combined with a wide ribbon and transparent glass beads: durable and fashion-conscious. "
d8e61402-b4e8-4c50-ba21-d804e5cdeb82.title: Horsepower

e0da0f1b-671a-425a-b1f8-7d5dfbcf0b75.body:
"This apron was used for work, and it shows! It is full of stains, tears and small holes. And when the apron tore right next to the ties, the wearer neatly repaired it with a few stitches so it could be used again. The detail photo also shows how the buttonhole was finished by hand with buttonhole stitches around it.

The apron has not been washed or restored, because these signs of use are part of the object's history and deserve to be seen."
e0da0f1b-671a-425a-b1f8-7d5dfbcf0b75.title: Stains, tears and old repairs

e773a1e5-3593-42f0-bf8a-bcda0d8767c1.body:
"Workwear has to be practical, so the sleeves are wide and have a cuff that opens so they can be rolled up. The apron is also essential, forming a first barrier against dirt getting on your clothes. The clothes are made of natural materials such as cotton and wool. They were used for a long time, let out, taken in and endlessly mended.

In North Brabant, where the people in the countryside mainly lived off the land, there was no money for luxury fabrics and clothes. In the (staged) photo, the working people have clearly done their best to look as fresh as possible."
e773a1e5-3593-42f0-bf8a-bcda0d8767c1.title: Rolling up your sleeves

87b3f4f9-fbf1-49c0-b814-b75374b53958.body: "You'd wish you had sound with this! The little legs of Van der Leest's Stripy Beast are bells. If you set the necklace down as an object you wouldn't notice, but when it is worn you can sometimes hear the bells softly jingling. As a whole, especially because of the soft textile it is crocheted from and its round shape, the necklace also looks like an oversized baby rattle. Felieke van der Leest often makes sure her work is both wearable and can be displayed as an object. That is why we photographed it both ways."
87b3f4f9-fbf1-49c0-b814-b75374b53958.title: Rattle

88d17de2-cf74-4ef8-925c-921d5952e75a.body: "Felieke van der Leest learned needlework techniques such as crocheting and knitting from her mother. When she started training as a goldsmith, she found it difficult, and perhaps almost inappropriate, to use these skills in her work as an artist. Contemporary jewellery was already using more and more unusual materials such as plastic and paper, but combining the traditional character of needlework with contemporary jewellery seemed almost incompatible. Her teacher at the Rietveld Academy, Ruudt Peters, encouraged Van der Leest to use her skilful crochet work in her art after all. Her graduation project, full of crocheted and knitted jewellery, caused a stir straight away!"
88d17de2-cf74-4ef8-925c-921d5952e75a.title: Crocheted jewellery

96a83c0b-162d-4755-b4a7-db73dc32f3ae.body: "Could it be that Felieke van der Leest makes so much work with animals in it because she grew up near Emmen Zoo? Like many teenage girls she loved horses, so she had a strong interest in animals from an early age. As an adult she mainly works plastic animals and crocheted ones into her work. These are often animals in miniature size, or, as in this case, rather large. But the stories she tells with them do not just belong in the nursery: she gives her animal figures an identity of their own, with lots of humour and a touch of absurdism."
96a83c0b-162d-4755-b4a7-db73dc32f3ae.title: All kinds of creatures

206468af-492c-4761-bbcf-1ad124262062.body:
"Unexpected and playful details are a trademark of the Brussels couture house Norine. This blouse has four bow trimmings down the centre front made of so-called grosgrain ribbon or petersham.

This material makes us think more of a hatband, the decorative band around the crown of a hat. Norine also used grosgrain ribbon for other surprising purposes, such as skirt waistbands. That is the case with the skirt of this ensemble, as well as with two other skirts from this couture house in the MoMu collection."
206468af-492c-4761-bbcf-1ad124262062.title: Grosgrain ribbon reinvented

3a45a7d6-3f00-dfbd-e836-b19b0cd93fb7.body:
"What stands out in this ensemble is the contrast between the textures of the blouse and skirt fabrics. The blouse is a fine silk in twill weave, the skirt a coarser linen in plain weave, and the simple cut of the skirt brings out its strong texture even more.

A white version of the same skirt is also in the MoMu collection, and it too is combined with a smooth-textured blouse. The combination of fabrics and cuts shows both the attention to the qualities of the fabric and the playfulness of the couture house's avant-garde signature.
3a45a7d6-3f00-dfbd-e836-b19b0cd93fb7.title: A love of coarsely woven fabrics

b83bbe87-7e28-15c2-e262-1b429116b8b9.body:
"At first glance, the pattern of this blouse is nothing special: a regular pattern of small motifs that vary in shape and colour. But look carefully and you will see a French word under each motif. They are words like chapeau, montagne, jolie, jeune. They throw us off, because there is no link between word and motif. It is deliberately absurd. 

The maker of the blouse, the Brussels couture house Norine, the French Fauvist and textile designer Raoul Dufy and the Belgian Surrealist painter René Magritte were close friends. Could the pattern be the result of a collaboration between the three? No other garments with this pattern are known so far."
b83bbe87-7e28-15c2-e262-1b429116b8b9.title: Surrealism meets couture

177261fe-9ede-4815-8a8a-280572ec90c5.body: "The skirt may look plain next to the embroidered sleeves, but it is just as impressive. Its fullness hides hundreds of pieces of cloth. It is made of narrow triangular inserts, called godets, sewn side by side. Together they give the skirt its volume, making it swing and flare as the wearer moves. Dresses like these can have more than 350 godets, and some as many as 800. Counting them all would take a while, and the maker had to cut and join every one by hand, a testament to the time spent on making it."
177261fe-9ede-4815-8a8a-280572ec90c5.title: One panel at a time

55b49b0a-74bc-4976-bb22-39269599923e.body:
"You can almost hear this dress. It is covered in buttons and metal pendants that would have clinked as its wearer moved, a sound that was sometimes believed to keep evil spirits away.

Buttons, coins and charms like these were often collected and added over the years, so a dress like this also recorded its owner's wealth and connections. They also help historians: stamped buttons and dated coins can sometimes reveal when and where a dress was decorated. This type of decorations and dress is common to a whole region ranging from Northern Pakistan to Afghanistan."
55b49b0a-74bc-4976-bb22-39269599923e.title: Sounds of a dress

aaebdc04-1b1d-4f41-a88c-9a8de49533b3.body: "The sleeves of this dress are exquisitely hand embroidered: what seems like woven cloth is actually embroidery, worked stitch by stitch in silk thread. The maker used tiny cross stitches and darning stitches, to build up fine motifs of red, orange, yellow and purple. Zigzags, stepped diamonds and hooked shapes repeat in stripes, and small red stars are scattered across the darker bands. This type of dress was probably embroidered by the woman who wore it or her relatives, over much time."
aaebdc04-1b1d-4f41-a88c-9a8de49533b3.title: Fine embroidery

764731de-0b6b-4070-a6c2-16efee94b877.body: "This dress is knitted in four colours of yarn from the Tilburg recycling company Wolkat: black, purple, blue and white. Their yarns are spun from discarded textiles. The collected textiles determine the colour and fibre content of the yarn, which means the yarns have not been (re)dyed."
764731de-0b6b-4070-a6c2-16efee94b877.title: Yarns from rags

c762665b-88c3-473e-a6cc-97c4fd58edd1.body: "To achieve these volumes in the dress, the TextielLab's knitting technician faced the challenge of developing knits that stretch but are also stiff enough. The combination of the knitted rib, which gives stretch, with Wolkat's stiff felt, invisibly worked into the inside, creates these parabolic volumes."
c762665b-88c3-473e-a6cc-97c4fd58edd1.title: Parabolic volumes

052d02f0-e793-fc78-9e5a-8585eb7f2321.body: "Just a small edge of a headdress peeps out from under the white veil. Married women from Hindeloopen wore a so-called ‘foarflechter’ over their under-cap: a cylindrical tube covered with red baize and trimmed with a lokkesnoor ribbon. The woman's long braided hair was rolled up in this tube."
052d02f0-e793-fc78-9e5a-8585eb7f2321.title: Foarflechter

0fffa1c1-f1bd-e858-26d5-cb37fcb98866.body:
"Curious to see more of the regional dress of Hindeloopen? For the film project 'Community Dressing', Theodorus Johannes researched this dress and recorded the dressing process with present-day wearers from Hindeloopen.

‘Community Dressing’ is a series of documentary videos about Dutch regional dress. By putting these almost lost costumes at the centre and questioning their traditions, norms, values, origins and disappearance, it offers a view from regional dress on the present-day fashion system."
0fffa1c1-f1bd-e858-26d5-cb37fcb98866.title: From head to toe

2804c28e-5ef0-e5f3-c2b7-8bb3574ea718.body: "Do you know why this lacing needle is hidden here? The lacing needle in the Hindeloopen costume has above all a practical function. With it, the woman threads the lace through her stays, a kind of corset. After use she sticks the gold or silver needle between the lacing, which turns it into a decorative piece of jewellery . With the position of the lacing needle, the wearer gives a subtle signal about her marital status: an unmarried woman wears the lacing needle on the left and a married woman on the right.”
2804c28e-5ef0-e5f3-c2b7-8bb3574ea718.title: The secret code of the lacing needle

444a014a-3dd2-0c33-4de7-3320fbcf206e.body: "A visible sign that a woman in Hindeloopen is about to marry is the colour of her wentke, a long coat worn open. From the eighteenth century, this typical Hindeloopen garment was made of chintz, a painted or printed cotton with multicoloured floral motifs from India. The bridal wentke is made of ‘milk-and-blood chintz’, with red flowers on a white ground."
444a014a-3dd2-0c33-4de7-3320fbcf206e.title: Milk-and-blood wentke

50177aef-00a0-3eea-bfcc-d51b10d44825.body:
"The chintz fabric you see here has become characteristic of Hindeloopen regional dress. But it travelled a long way before it ended up here.

Episode VI of Community Dressing explores the widespread use of chintz, the Indian hand-painted or printed cotton, in Hindeloopen dress. The film takes you to the origins of chintz, highlights the trade relationship between the Netherlands and India, and shows the influence this textile still has on our fashion system today."
50177aef-00a0-3eea-bfcc-d51b10d44825.title: The journey of chintz

86ac01d4-934e-cf56-4f1d-de1439c8a2b6.body:
"In Friesland the chatelaine is also called a ‘prak’, a term that refers to its practical nature. From the silver or gold hook with chains hang useful objects such as scissors, a needle case and a pincushion, so the sewing kit is always at hand.

The precious chatelaine was a popular wedding gift and served not only as a handy tool but also as a status symbol for the wearer. What do you think these objects mean?”
86ac01d4-934e-cf56-4f1d-de1439c8a2b6.title: A 'prak': for practical things

b242f593-40a6-b78c-fbbc-516df95d71a3.body:
"The veil is essential for a Hindeloopen bride. This square white veil of fine linen goes over the foarflechter. Tassels braided from white thread, called akertjes, hang from its corners. Wearing this veil, the woman is ‘in het wit snoer’ (in the white cord) and recognisable as a bride.

This painting, 'Putting on the bridal veil in Hindeloopen', shows a Hindeloopen bride having her traditional veil put on. This ritual was an important moment in the bride's life.

In the painting, the young bride, Griet Eekma, sits while an older woman carefully fastens her veil. The veil symbolises the passage into marriage and was put on by older, experienced women as part of the wedding."
b242f593-40a6-b78c-fbbc-516df95d71a3.title: Putting on the bridal veil

e963147d-1d90-a3d8-2ad3-fd712fa5366c.body:
“Here hangs a frame bag: a fabric bag attached to a silver or gold frame. A separate hook lets the bag be fastened to the belt or skirt band. Although the frame bag appears both in towns and in the countryside in the 18th century, in the 19th century it becomes a common element in Dutch regional dress, including the Hindeloopen costume.

Biblical scenes are popular as decoration for the frame; this one shows the Last Supper in the middle.”
e963147d-1d90-a3d8-2ad3-fd712fa5366c.title: A showy frame bag

43e3a093-e7c2-4171-a5ca-c2d1d8c18c07.body:
"Inspired by the Jacobean flower on this chintz skirt, we got to work at the Zaans Museum during a masterclass organised by Crafts Council as part of the Jimmy Nelson exhibition Ode to the Netherlands (2024).

I translated the floral motifs into an embroidery pattern that the participants could work with themselves. Using different embroidery stitches and colourful threads, they gave the design their own twist.

By combining classic motifs with modern materials and techniques, unique embroideries were created for contemporary garments: personal, creative and with a nod to the craft of the past. Just like the embroiderers of centuries ago, every maker put their own stamp on the result."
43e3a093-e7c2-4171-a5ca-c2d1d8c18c07.title: Flower embroidery at the Zaans Museum

f1ad1207-9b8a-4e94-800f-dd626ba25792.body:
"Following this 360° recording, this chintz skirt served as the inspiration for a contemporary embroidery project at the Zaans Museum, centred on three themes that mattered to me:

Floral motifs as a fashion statement
In the 18th century, chintz fabrics with lively floral patterns were loved by fashion icons. These bright motifs, typical of the traditional dress of the Zaan region, have been brought back to life in modern fashion.  

Sustainability
The original chintz fabrics, made in India, were remarkably colourfast and durable. They stayed bright even after frequent washing, thanks to a dyeing process unknown in Europe. Their light and strong qualities made them so popular that they were banned in England and France to protect the local wool and linen industries.  

Jacobean techniques
Although chintz was made in India, the floral motifs were adapted to European taste and inspired by the heavy wool embroidery of the Jacobean style."
f1ad1207-9b8a-4e94-800f-dd626ba25792.title: The Jacobean flower as inspiration

32498221-97c6-4cb6-839d-d35358fe6d79.body: "In the 1970s, Anouk Damoiseaux's mother and father, together with other parents, founded the 'Anti-Autoritaire Kresj' (Anti-Authoritarian Crèche) for their children. They wanted their children to have an anti-authoritarian upbringing. The parents took turns looking after the children, who were allowed to do whatever they liked. In this way the children had to explore their own limits. The idea was that through this upbringing they would recognise coercion later in life and resist it. The ultimate goal was a utopian society."
32498221-97c6-4cb6-839d-d35358fe6d79.title: Anti-Authoritarian Crèche

4b17cabf-9220-4385-8f4c-9036b8c427d6.body:
"Besides emotional reasons, people also cherish their clothes out of sheer necessity. When body shapes change, for example through pregnancy or a growing waistline, clothes are regularly altered and let out so they can be worn again. When there is no money for new trousers, the old pair is endlessly mended. This was often done as invisibly as possible, because darned holes were seen as a sign of poverty, something people were ashamed of.

That mending can also be an expression of creativity is shown by the children's clothes of Marga Groen . In the 1970s she wore corduroy trousers with contrasting patches on the knees, a jumper made from leftover scraps of different coloured knitting wool, and a handmade jacket. Marga's colourful and creatively mended children's clothes show the renewed appreciation for handwork, in which this form of cherishing is seen as an expression of individuality and personal expression."
4b17cabf-9220-4385-8f4c-9036b8c427d6.title: Creative cherishing

878249f8-6eb1-4a50-82b8-de5573e7361b.body:
"Can you see what the artist is trying to show here with a black and a white person in the water?

With this, Scott criticises the stereotype that black people cannot swim. It has its roots in a history of exclusion and racism. In the United States, black people were for a long time denied access to public swimming pools, or only allowed into badly neglected ones. During segregation pools were actively separated, and discrimination continued after it was abolished. As a result, many black children never had swimming lessons, which led to gaps in swimming skills lasting generations.

This structural injustice lives on in persistent stereotypes with tragic consequences. In The Swimming Lesson, Joyce Scott refers to this painful history and shows how exclusion can literally lead to vulnerability in the water."
878249f8-6eb1-4a50-82b8-de5573e7361b.title: Not being able to swim

f3ad43b7-b1d6-4158-8da1-10ed51ef1aa6.body:
"Take a close look at this object: can you see how the beads have been sewn together one by one with thread?

The peyote stitch is a bead-weaving technique from Indigenous North American cultures, including the Huichol, Lakota and Navajo. It was traditionally used for ceremonial objects in the Native American Church. Small, even glass beads are sewn together with needle and thread in a zigzag pattern. The weaving is done without a loom (off-loom) and produces a supple, textile-like fabric.

Joyce Scott uses this technique to create detailed, three-dimensional shapes. By carefully controlling the direction of the pattern and the tension of the thread, she builds faces, bodies and other figures entirely out of beads."
f3ad43b7-b1d6-4158-8da1-10ed51ef1aa6.title: 3D technique with beads

3443ebd5-4726-12a7-808f-dfe8f2b99fdf.body:
"We turned this armour into a 'digital twin' and brought it to life through the very first 3D scans of metal in the Netherlands. Countless try-outs let us test different software; in the end we even used separate programs for the breastplate and the shoulder pieces. By experimenting we reached the result we wanted, and put together our own ‘Frankenstein workflow’.

The project Skeuomorphia (2024), made for the exhibition Unboxing: Fashion from the Archives at the Amsterdam Museum, explored the evolution of form and function in fashion through a ceremonial suit of armour from the Amsterdam Museum.

The film links skeuomorphism (the reuse of old forms) to deimatic behaviour in nature, where appearance is manipulated for effect. Just like animals, people use clothing to make an impression. Through lighting and digital manipulation of the scans, new layers are added to the story."
3443ebd5-4726-12a7-808f-dfe8f2b99fdf.title: A digital twin

561efa88-eb4e-b619-0ec5-a6b92ba5c9e0.body:
"The armour exaggerates the shape of the 'perfect' male body to express ideas of masculinity, such as strength and protection, but also wealth and status. A men's jerkin carries the same design language, but in a more wearable material than metal.

In our digital project Skeuomorphia (2024-) we found that metal armour seems to be a starting point for men's fashion. Look at how the torso is divided and how it is designed to transfer (translate) the male shape into a new object and emphasise it: that is skeuomorphism."
561efa88-eb4e-b619-0ec5-a6b92ba5c9e0.title: The perfect male body

592f74d3-e3e1-9a17-9715-b2c087c9a7ce.body:
"The illustrations and decorations on this breastplate were made with an etching technique. In the 1570s, the Amsterdam civic guard ordered many suits of armour like this one from northern Italy. This one was probably made in Brescia.

The figures are often classical or biblical figures such as Mars or Judith. This medallion, showing a kind of tower, represents either the anonymous engraver or the workshop. What other illustrations can you discover?"
592f74d3-e3e1-9a17-9715-b2c087c9a7ce.title: Etching technique

8f29457b-4c86-106e-1102-5578a9ac7d3d.body:
"This breastplate is part of a so-called Pisan half-armour, made up of ten different pieces to protect every part of the body. The armour was worn by the infantry of the civic guard: soldiers on foot. They had to protect the city walls and gates and keep order in Amsterdam. 

During the annual fair in September, the guardsmen showed themselves to the city in full, shining armour. As firearms became more powerful, armour gradually became more of a status symbol than protection. Another theory is that this armour was left behind by the Spanish after Amsterdam went over to the Reformed side in 1578."
8f29457b-4c86-106e-1102-5578a9ac7d3d.title: In full, shining armour at the annual fair

9e80474e-3fea-21a3-4d0e-efae870e41ab.body:
"If you zoom in, you can find rust on the metal. But there is much more rust that you can hardly see with the naked eye, but that does show up on the diffuse map of the 3D model made on the computer.

The photos we took of the armour for the digital 'Skeuomorphia' project are free of reflections and showed, for example, much more rust. There was even an imperfection caused by a piece of tape someone had once stuck on it. For conservation and restoration work this is very valuable information. New digital techniques play an important role here and make you look at an object differently."
9e80474e-3fea-21a3-4d0e-efae870e41ab.title: Hidden rust

b1ac3c0b-788e-6aaa-c0ab-8b831bd87e8f.body:
"At the Amsterdam Museum, the 16th-century breastplate was shown outside its historical context for the first time. During the exhibition Grand March: A Historic House through a Ballroom (2023-2024), in collaboration with House of Vineyard, the first ballroom house in the Netherlands, the rooms of the Willet-Holthuysen House underwent radical fashion and art interventions that highlighted the power of ballroom culture .

In the splendour of the Grand Salon, once the setting of 19th-century balls, Ball Beyond the Binary was presented. In this installation, the breastplate stands for the need for protection of the LGBTIQ+ community, Black and of colour."
b1ac3c0b-788e-6aaa-c0ab-8b831bd87e8f.title: Protection for the ballroom community

06bd9629-b3cd-a19a-a617-951b0e542c39.body:
"The back of a doublet can consist of two back panels with a centre-back seam or one back panel without a centre-back seam.

This doublet has a back panel in one piece. Because leather is stiffer than fabric and harder to shape, a dart has been cut out of the leather to follow the shape of the back. The edges of the cut-out have been laid against each other and sewn together, with the edge facing outwards."
06bd9629-b3cd-a19a-a617-951b0e542c39.title: The shape of the back

26bd9ee3-0739-5cbb-9e2b-e002dc3614a5.body:
"Can you count how many buttonholes this doublet has?

Today, the button and buttonhole are a fixed part of our clothing. Yet this way of fastening only appeared in the Middle Ages and became more and more common in the 13th and 14th centuries.

On this doublet the fastening consists of 29 buttonholes. They are cut into the leather and finished with buttonhole stitch in thread. Only six of the pewter buttons are left."
26bd9ee3-0739-5cbb-9e2b-e002dc3614a5.title: Medieval buttons

7375c358-b002-ea29-bfe6-d21e5587a7fa.body:
"Take a good look at the worn little collar. Here we see the material linen: a much-used material for the insides and interlinings of old clothing.

Interlinings give a garment firmness and were worked into it in several layers. On this collar the leather has decayed so much that we can see the inside of the collar. The collar gets its shape from several layers of linen and is also lined with linen."
7375c358-b002-ea29-bfe6-d21e5587a7fa.title: A linen collar

f731b685-f159-aee8-da69-df1ebafab2b9.body:
"A doublet consists of two front panels, which run far under the armhole, and the back. The back can consist of two panels with a centre-back seam or one panel without a centre-back seam.

Visually, the front panel is divided in two by a decorative line running down from the armhole. Green woven decorative braids were originally sewn on here. If you zoom in closely, you can see that the stitch holes are still visible where the braid has disappeared."
f731b685-f159-aee8-da69-df1ebafab2b9.title: An extra decorative line

ffccf690-65ea-0f93-803b-0b44e869e5ba.body:
"Doublets could be made in many materials: plain wool or silk, but also luxurious woven fabrics.

This doublet is made of sheepskin leather. Leather is a practical material in daily life and on horseback. Besides the leather, the seams were finished with green woven silk braids, which have disappeared in many places.

The Kunstmuseum's collection includes a replica of this doublet. Why this replica was made is unknown."
ffccf690-65ea-0f93-803b-0b44e869e5ba.title: Leather: a practical material

07da462f-29e8-4eac-abe3-088f341a3f0a.body:
"During the German occupation of the Netherlands, Mies Boissevain helped Jewish people in hiding. In 1943 she was arrested. In prison, acquaintances gave her a scarf made of all kinds of fabric scraps. About this ‘patchwork scarf’, as she called it, she wrote: ‘All little scraps: bright, cheerful, colourful, fresh.’ It gave her strength, even after she was deported to the Ravensbrück concentration camp. ‘The patchwork scarf had long been taken from me. But my mind held on to the memory.’

Mies survived Ravensbrück, though she lost her two sons and her husband during the war. Back in the Netherlands, she was inspired by the patchwork scarf and designed the National Festive Skirt. On her own skirt she embroidered the date of her liberation and worked in pieces of her sons' clothing.

Shortly after the Second World War, the government set up a committee to decide how the liberation should be celebrated. Mies introduced the National Festive Skirt to this committee. All women in the Netherlands were called on to make such a skirt."
07da462f-29e8-4eac-abe3-088f341a3f0a.title: Mies's call

58aa2fb6-af56-48bb-b46b-f38a5a333e5c.body:
"Mies Boissevain-van Lennep called on women to have their skirt registered in the 'skirt register'. Only home-made skirts could be registered, to stop factory-made skirts from being produced. After registration the skirt was given a stamp with a registration number, as you can see on this skirt with 1940. The stamp reads 'De Nationale Feestrok' (The National Festive Skirt). Around it, though faded, you can read the text 'Saamgevoegd op één ondergrond' (Joined together on one base). In the middle is NI, short for Nationaal Instituut (National Institute).

After registration, the owner received a postcard with the registration number and the advice to embroider this number on the skirt. No embroidered registration number has been found on this skirt. In total about 4,000 festive skirts were registered, and there were probably many more unregistered ones. The skirt register itself, however, has never been found."
58aa2fb6-af56-48bb-b46b-f38a5a333e5c.title: Stamped in the register

a3a15bcf-2294-4a8b-a301-308ef9e3763e.body:
"In 1948 Elisabeth Maasdijk also wrote a song in tribute to the Liberation Skirt. It was sung at celebrations and parades, strengthening the symbolism: The Song of the National Festive Skirt."

Weave into your skirt the pattern of your life,
Women and girls of village and of town.
Shining symbol of women's striving,
Wear it with joy, as the flower wears its leaf.

Unity in a wealth of lines and colours,
Your skirt forms the bond that holds us together,
In the whole of historical events,
Adorn the design with your heart and your hand.

Stamp your skirt with the mark of your days,
Carry what Was and what Is in your banner.
Present and Past, cheerfully worn,
May they grace your dress, your family, your life.
a3a15bcf-2294-4a8b-a301-308ef9e3763e.title: The national festive skirt song

a3b3c05c-bb2f-45ab-b43d-47139714405a.body:
"At the first national celebration of Liberation Day on 5 May 1946, many women wore a National Festive Skirt. These skirts, made from scraps of old clothing and embroidered with important national and personal dates, symbolised the rebuilding of the Netherlands and the new harmonious society that had to be built together after the Second World War. The initiative came from resistance member Mies Boissevain-van Lennep, who hoped that women would keep wearing the skirt on national holidays as a symbol of connection and renewal.

To spread this ideal, a national propaganda campaign was set up, supported by a colourful poster. The enthusiasm turned out to be short-lived, however. After 1948 the National Festive Skirt gradually faded from view, a development that coincided with the growing silence about the war in the Netherlands.

A last highlight was the great skirt event during the parade on the Binnenhof in The Hague to mark Queen Wilhelmina's fifty-year jubilee on 2 September 1948. After that, Boissevain-van Lennep tried to spread the idea in the United States with the Liberation Skirt, which was received as a symbol of the struggle for world peace, but there too without lasting success."
a3b3c05c-bb2f-45ab-b43d-47139714405a.title: The harmonious society

a8e2dcff-b108-4494-bc73-b351d00c918d.body:
"The National Festive Skirt was more than a colourful garment: it came with clear rules. Its initiator, Mies Boissevain-van Lennep, decided that the skirt had to be made from old, colourful scraps sewn onto an existing skirt (patchwork). In this way the old base disappeared and something new was created: a symbol for the rebuilding of the Netherlands after the war.

The hem always had to consist of plain, isosceles triangles, starting with the date 5 May 1945, followed by the dates of the national holidays on which the skirt was worn. Important moments from personal life, both joyful and sad, could also be worked into the skirt later. In this way the patchwork could help women come to terms with their war experiences.

Wearing the skirts together created a sense of connection. Despite all the different fabrics, stories and backgrounds of the wearers, they carried the same message: 'Unity in diversity, new from old, building up from breaking down, and one dress makes unity.'"
a8e2dcff-b108-4494-bc73-b351d00c918d.title: A patchwork of rules

2b0b3e61-eb49-4592-bc7c-b5684cc7b4a9.body:
"This fabric was designed by Bas Kosters as part of a project by Textiel Factorij that explores the influence of Indian painted and hand-printed cotton fabrics, known as chintz, on Dutch regional dress.

These colourfast fabrics became hugely popular in the 17th and 18th centuries and were taken up into different regional dresses. At first they were mainly painted by hand with a bamboo pen, but because of the great demand in the West, the fabrics were also made with block printing so they could be produced faster.

The documentary Tracing the VOC by Jenne Sipman (2017) follows five Dutch artists and designers, including Bas Kosters, during the project and their collaboration with Indian craftspeople. Bas Kosters was commissioned to work with Adam Khatri to print fabrics. The challenge for Khatri was printing ‘without a system’: a random print.

The film offers both a historical perspective and a look at today's craft practices, in which centuries-old techniques are still passed down from generation to generation."
2b0b3e61-eb49-4592-bc7c-b5684cc7b4a9.title: Tracing the VOC - a project by Textiel Factorij

306e1c27-3d07-4402-a064-dfb97ac67902.body:
"This look, which has become part of the Zuiderzeemuseum's collection, was part of a larger collection by Bas Kosters: My Paper Crown. Kosters developed his own block-printed fabrics for this collection."

"The inspiration for this expressive collection came from different eras and continents, combining rococo and traditional African costume with workwear. The title of the collection, ‘My Paper Crown’, also reflected the importance of paying attention. After all, a paper crown is just as important as any other crown." - Bas Kosters
306e1c27-3d07-4402-a064-dfb97ac67902.title: 'My Paper Crown'

733668c7-66a7-41c8-9965-f49f9eb46dcd.body:
"Take a good look at the buttons on this design: shiny, decorative and strikingly placed. They may seem purely decorative, but they refer directly to the traditional fall-front trousers of fishermen from the Zuiderzee region.

For the silhouette, Bas Kosters was inspired by the historical fisherman's costume. In villages such as Urk and Volendam, men wore trousers closed with 'broekstukken' (trouser pieces): decorative buttons, often of silver or even old coins. On Urk the pieces were richly decorated with biblical scenes in relief, although that relief has often partly worn away from the heavy work on board.

This work was part of the exhibition Ambacht in Dracht (Craft in Costume, Zuiderzeemuseum, 2018), a collaboration with Textiel Factorij in which contemporary designers such as Kosters gave a present-day interpretation of chintz and regional dress."
733668c7-66a7-41c8-9965-f49f9eb46dcd.title: A tribute to the fishermen of the Zuiderzee

2396798a-7148-4c7e-a89c-23789b9fef81.body: "Agate is a slightly translucent semi-precious stone. Because of its variety of colour bands and frequent crystal inclusions, it is seen as a decorative stone. It can be polished glossy, satin or matt, and the last is the case in this piece. The matt surface makes the stone feel soft, as if you are touching skin. This strengthens the connection between the jewellery and the body even more."
2396798a-7148-4c7e-a89c-23789b9fef81.title: Matt agate

abac36b4-e395-4a3a-bd0b-9323de77fa7a.body:
"With this wearable Adam's apple of agate, Sari Räthel wants to offer the chance to put yourself in a different body. You wear this piece around your neck, with the agate Adam's apple under your chin, against your throat. Räthel was inspired by gender theory:"

Gender theorist Judith Butler claims that gender is a social construction we are born into and copy from our parents and surroundings, but not something we necessarily have a choice about how we enact in life. This project is interrogating this idea by enabling the wearer to ‘try on’ their gender in a fictional wardrobe full of jewellery items, which embody stereotypically gendered body parts. Offering them the accessories to change it or enhance it, depending on how they feel or want to appear. The pieces are inspired by breasts, hips, balls, broad shoulder and the Adam’s apple but also adorn areas which normally get cosmetically modified to fit into social expectations like the armpit, the nails and the ear canal. - Sarah Räthel
abac36b4-e395-4a3a-bd0b-9323de77fa7a.title: What does an Adam's apple feel like?
