289924b5-e7fc-45b8-a4aa-12a07bb84bc0.body:
"The Exhibition of Historical Clothing took place in November 1919 on the ground floor of the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam. The event was an initiative to show historical garments in display cases, such as 18th-century gowns and this gown, then still described as a crinoline from 1850. The proceeds went to a good cause: the Society for Improving the Lot of the Blind, an organisation that worked for blind and partially sighted people.

This archive photo of the exhibition gave us a valuable look at how the ensemble was displayed at the time. With the help of this photo we were able to dress this special collection object again, probably for the last time, because the ensemble is currently in a very fragile condition. After lying in a storage drawer for decades, the gown was mounted once more to reconstruct it from 2D to 3D . This way the gown can live on in digital eternity."
289924b5-e7fc-45b8-a4aa-12a07bb84bc0.title: On show in 1919

474dd753-70e4-6278-b27e-a7ec6b735880.body:
"Can you see the wear on the bottom edge of this dress? It looks like this gown was walked in a lot, through parks and streets.

In the second half of the 19th century, walking and outdoor leisure became more and more popular, especially among the middle and upper classes. It was seen as a healthy and respectable way to spend time. The rise of public parks and promenades in cities gave women the chance to walk in public. In Amsterdam this became possible on a large scale when the Vondelpark opened in 1865."
474dd753-70e4-6278-b27e-a7ec6b735880.title: Walking: a popular pastime

84c6a021-c2a4-2e9e-959b-f9acacb58f53.body:
"Can you see the little loops here? Lifting the skirt had a practical reason: protecting the long skirts from mud, dust and dirt while walking. This was especially important on unpaved roads or wet paths.

The skirts were draped using ribbons, loops or buttons, sometimes sewn to the waist or the sides of the gown. On this walking dress, the overskirt was buttoned up with loops. These prints show other examples of overskirts being lifted."
84c6a021-c2a4-2e9e-959b-f9acacb58f53.title: Lifting the skirts

0c4d6198-da12-445f-8568-e2d3f60b0f37.body:
"The cap closes at the front with two white cotton twill tapes, sewn to the underside of the crown. The separate bow is slid over the chin tapes as decoration. 

Originally there was no separate decorative bow; these were two separate chin ribbons that closed the cap. At some point the two starched ribbons were tied in advance, sewn in place and used as a separate bow. This guaranteed the wearer an impeccable bow."
0c4d6198-da12-445f-8568-e2d3f60b0f37.title: An impeccable bow

508d0eee-3dab-448f-9eab-81477e7fcb85.body:
"A so-called droefmuts with a separate decorative bow, worn by a girl or woman in the regional dress of the north-west Veluwe. The cap was acquired in Oldebroek.

A droefmuts was worn on weekdays when people wanted to be smartly dressed, for example when going out or to catechism (religious instruction). This is also called opknapdracht (smart dress), a variant of regional dress that sits between everyday dress and Sunday or occasion dress in how it presents. Opknapdracht was worn, for example, for weekday visits or going to the market.

This type of cap appeared in several regional dresses in the eastern Netherlands. In every town or region the cap had small differences and a different name. In Nunspeet, for example, an almost identical version was worn that was called a floddermuts there."
508d0eee-3dab-448f-9eab-81477e7fcb85.title: A droefmuts for smart dress

a2f73588-818e-4636-bf9a-e0842e591f75.body:
"Droefmutsen were made by specialist cap makers. It took special knowledge and skill to starch and pleat these caps.

The crown is of machine-made cotton lace. Along the front edge are three pleated front strips. On top of the cap is a trimming of pleated lace and ribbon folded into so-called 'snail shells'. At the back, a fan-folded strip has been added, made of starched white cotton edged with machine-made lace.
a2f73588-818e-4636-bf9a-e0842e591f75.title: Cap makers

1141a46e-5bb4-d889-4ca6-84477a5a2e49.body:
"The silver bag frame of this frame bag was originally a purse frame. A silver skirt hook is attached to the top of the frame with two small silver jaseron chains.

The frame bears the maker's mark of the Leeuwarden silversmith H. van Assen, who worked from 1830 to 1875. On the front is the date letter E for 1839. On top of the frame is a standard mark: a small lion walking to the right with the number 2 below it. The clip of the skirt hook bears the letter J, a tax mark from the period 1906-1953.

Matching motif
The linen bag is decorated with multicoloured embroidery. The motifs are embroidered by hand in a so-called satin stitch. The bag is lined with white satin."
1141a46e-5bb4-d889-4ca6-84477a5a2e49.title: Bag frame or purse frame?

42cc7400-bf9e-4b2f-9f63-561a19c871b9.body:
"This New Frisian Costume was made by Jo Kars-Stienstra for Afke Wiersma. Afke worked as a secretary at the office of the FAF (Fryske Ambachts- en Folkskunst, Frisian Crafts and Folk Art). The FAF was a foundation that acted as a go-between for craftspeople and sellers of handmade products. Afke wore the costume at official FAF meetings and at shows that Jo Kars organised to promote the New Frisian Costume.

Jo Kars was a member of the New Frisian Costume Committee and one of the most important promoters of the New Frisian Costume. As early as the 1940s, Jo researched Frisian regional dress and worked elements of Dutch regional dress into her own designs. At the Committee's request, she designed four of the ten trial costumes presented in Leeuwarden on 21 September 1950."
42cc7400-bf9e-4b2f-9f63-561a19c871b9.title: Jo Kars-Stienstra

968c7307-412a-f355-f517-f3a6e4495ba3.body: "The so-called New Frisian Costume was introduced in 1950 as an attempt to create a new Frisian regional dress . After the Second World War, Frisian regional dress had almost disappeared as everyday wear. Around 1950 it was mainly still worn as folklore dress at events. For this, people liked to go back to the Frisian regional dress of the middle of the nineteenth century."
968c7307-412a-f355-f517-f3a6e4495ba3.title: New Frisian Costume

a65f62c3-67b0-41bb-aec2-7ef49630bacd.body:
"The fichu (shoulder scarf) and apron of the so-called New Frisian Costume go back to the Frisian costume of the mid-nineteenth century. This was seen as the heyday of Frisian dress.  

Both the fichu and the apron are made of white cotton batiste. Threads have been grouped together along the length and width of the weave, creating squares of 6.5 by 6.5 centimetres. A border of whitework embroidery runs along the hems."
a65f62c3-67b0-41bb-aec2-7ef49630bacd.title: Batiste fichu

d66ff4a3-f0d7-6eac-9db1-daaed74c5175.body:
"Together with the Fries Landbouwblad (a Frisian farming magazine), the committee published embroidery patterns designed by Jo Kars-Stienstra. With these, the wearer could decorate her New Frisian Costume and also show something of her personal background: clover and ears of corn for farmers' wives, for example, and violets for town dwellers.

The cap and the frame bag of this New Frisian Costume are decorated with multicoloured embroidery. The motifs are embroidered by hand in a so-called satin stitch."
d66ff4a3-f0d7-6eac-9db1-daaed74c5175.title: An embroidery pattern for everyone

dc01a5ab-5366-10dd-d60a-324b54d5340a.body:
"The silhouette of the New Frisian Costume is based on the so-called New Look. This style comes from the French fashion designer Christian Dior (1905-1957). He launched his first fashion collection in February 1947, which went down in history as the New Look. Typical of this style were the narrow waist and the full skirt.

Some parts of the New Frisian Costume, such as the peplum of the jacket, are based on older Frisian dress."
dc01a5ab-5366-10dd-d60a-324b54d5340a.title: The New Look

f6d23bcc-8fa6-84c9-3452-173c4146e728.body:
"Can you tell what kind of fabric this is? The jacket and skirt are made of so-called ‘Ploeg fabric’, a strong, good-quality woven fabric. Ploeg fabrics were made at the De Ploeg weaving mill in Bergeijk. The mill was part of the cooperative production and consumption society ‘De Ploeg’, which was founded on idealistic principles. The mill became known for its good-quality clothing and furnishing fabrics."

Written by Jacco Hooikammer
f6d23bcc-8fa6-84c9-3452-173c4146e728.title: Ploeg fabric

1ba09c6f-78a3-4d20-acd7-f675d76d2fa7.body: "Fully in line with the fashion of the 1820s, the ivory silk gown has a narrow, slightly raised waist, a low shoulder and neckline and a cone-shaped skirt. Both the bodice and the hem are richly decorated with satin, tulle and rouleaux. This gown is a fine example of a transitional period in fashion, showing features of both the Empire (raised waist, low shoulder and neckline) and the Restoration (cone-shaped skirt and a richly decorated hem)."
1ba09c6f-78a3-4d20-acd7-f675d76d2fa7.title: Empire or Restoration?

4655c660-1037-2e52-274c-37b1b87b8627.body:
"Both the bodice and the skirt of the gown are very richly decorated. On the front and back of the bodice you can see a row of cylindrical rolled strips of fabric that run down from the shoulders in a V shape and are held together at the front by a pleated piece of silk.

These so-called rouleaux also frame the neckline and the puff sleeves, both finished with a tulle edge. The rouleaux at the neckline are decorated with a triangular piece of plain silk. This pattern returns on the back of the gown."
4655c660-1037-2e52-274c-37b1b87b8627.title: Rouleaux: rolled strips of fabric

49d2b2f2-3adb-492a-9aab-bdac544384fd.body:
"If you look at the gown up close, you can see all kinds of interesting details in the fabric. It consists of alternating shiny and matt vertical stripes. The matt stripes are very finely woven and have a transparent striped pattern. 

On the shiny stripes you can see a pattern of flower sprigs running along the whole length of the fabric. The skirt of the gown is pleated at the top, so the vertical stripes on the bodice and skirt do not line up. Thanks to the shiny ivory silk, the gown almost seems to glow!"
49d2b2f2-3adb-492a-9aab-bdac544384fd.title: Shining silk

8cc3d595-43ed-47d5-be20-06169e8ef9bd.body: "The skirt of the gown has a hem of pleated white satin. Above it, satin appliqués have been sewn on diagonally all the way round. These are edged with tulle. The inner edge of the appliqués is decorated with silver-coloured glass beads. The decorations give the skirt more volume and help create the fashionable silhouette of the 1820s."
8cc3d595-43ed-47d5-be20-06169e8ef9bd.title: Decorated hem

bcc035f0-2c51-cffa-a6be-be96e2593d82.body:
"In 1937 Museum Dordrecht received a gift of clothing through the well-known Dordrecht writer Top Naeff (1878-1953), including this small ivory gown with matching silk shoes. In her accompanying letter, Naeff wrote that according to family tradition this was the wedding dress of a ‘great-great-great-grandmother’.

This may have been Anne Cornelie van Wageningen (1800-1857), who married Jacob Staets Vriesendorp (1800-1863) in 1824. They were the parents of Simon van Gijn's wife Cornelia and the great-grandparents of Top.

She doubted that it was a wedding dress, though: “(...) judging by the matching shoes, she must have been undersized for a bride.’’ She thought it was more likely a ball gown."

Excerpt from the publication 'Dordrecht in de mode: 1700-1950', 2019.
bcc035f0-2c51-cffa-a6be-be96e2593d82.title: Shoes for dancing?

03e2eb73-93e0-4e5c-b52d-c0de514c6bf2.body:
"Ripped clothes, safety pins and paint: that must be punk! But imagine how shocking this iconic look must have been when punk culture emerged. Punk is much more than a fashion statement; it is rebellion in style.

These elements challenge ideas about neatness: here, social norms, conformity and consumerism are broken in plain sight. And the ripped clothing, held together and decorated again with all kinds of materials, shows punk's DIY (do-it-yourself) creativity.

At the same time, the style has a clearly raw and aggressive edge, with which it also rejects the commercialised hippie subculture and the hedonism of disco."
03e2eb73-93e0-4e5c-b52d-c0de514c6bf2.title: Do It Yourself

394d8856-97e2-4d76-8ed3-feedf9e57abf.body:
"Can you see from the badges what this punk stood for? For the exhibition Jong! Jongerencultuur en stijl in Nederland 1950-2000’ at Museum Rotterdam (2000), several punks were interviewed":

"Punks were against nuclear power, racism, religion, materialism, capitalism, the police and the royal family, “against the system of people who want to make a lot of money.” They rebelled against society, for example by squatting and protesting. “Life was shit, you definitely shouldn't fall into line.” The anti-society attitude was summed up in the slogan “Fuck the System”. Another well-known slogan was “No more Future.” “In the early eighties it really was a bit ‘No more Future’. Everything was going down economically.. […] The resistance against society had a strongly aggressive tone. “The idea was also that you looked extreme and behaved extremely.”
394d8856-97e2-4d76-8ed3-feedf9e57abf.title: No More Future

b1a720f2-72ae-5bb9-afc8-b2d4a1cbe847.body:
"Punk stands for rejecting the well-behaved consumer society, but contradictorily it also seems to have been shaped by clever marketing.

The rise and style of punk are closely linked to Malcolm McLaren and fashion legend Vivienne Westwood. In the 1970s they opened their boutique SEX in London, selling provocative clothing. McLaren also set up the influential punk band the Sex Pistols to promote the rebellious look. Their defiant anti-establishment attitude, music and clothing hit like a bomb. Other bands, boutiques and clothing brands followed.

One example is Modzart, the brand of these trousers. As a true punk, the wearer completely customised the jeans."
b1a720f2-72ae-5bb9-afc8-b2d4a1cbe847.title: Buy yourself rebellious?

d46ec86b-4c1e-4319-bf86-6fe62c275015.body:
"The black leather jacket was an important part of a punk outfit, as interviews with punks for the exhibition Jong! Jongerencultuur en stijl in Nederland 1950-2000’ (Young! Youth culture and style in the Netherlands 1950-2000) at Museum Rotterdam (2000) show":

"The main item of the punk wardrobe was the leather jacket, usually black. “Everyone had a leather jacket, but everyone's leather jacket was different. You put all sorts of things on it … I bought it in a second-hand shop … for 25 guilders you could get a nice jacket.” “For those jackets especially: the more worked on, the better. “If it could stand up, if you could just stand it somewhere, those were the best jackets.” Punks also wore a lot of T-shirts, but they were adapted to punk fashion. “T-shirts … the sleeves came off and the neck was cut out.”
d46ec86b-4c1e-4319-bf86-6fe62c275015.title: A unique jacket and T-shirt

8c69bc32-441f-40ff-8f0d-6fc742554dc7.body:
"Let your eye be carried along by the wavy, psychedelic print of this blouse: light and dark blue, yellow, orange, brown and black dance over a white ground, in which the name ‘Rich Mnisi’ is subtly worked.

Rich Mnisi designs many of his garments to be gender-neutral. Mnisi named this blouse The Waves. The blouse itself has a classic cut, with a stand-up collar, long sleeves with cuffs, and a front opening with silver-coloured metal press studs. In his collection Hiya Kaya this striking print returns in several garments, including a pair of trousers."
8c69bc32-441f-40ff-8f0d-6fc742554dc7.title: 'The Wave'

acd2fad0-7bb2-4756-bf86-06db8b0bb76a.body:
"To promote the Hiya Kaya collection, a short film was made as a tribute to the VaTsonga tribe. In the film you see the traditionally knotted skirts that inspired this design dancing: a celebration of the female form.

A quote from Rich Mnisi: Our collection is not only a celebration of the tribe, but specifically her women. The collection is a call-to-action for the protection of women, especially our mothers. [...] Open your eyes and be transported to a scene in a Tsonga village, where the women are throngs of a recital of their world-renowned twist dance – a dance which involves vigorous pelvis gyrations driven by core strength and stamina."
acd2fad0-7bb2-4756-bf86-06db8b0bb76a.title: A celebration of VaTsonga

be8bf109-5677-4714-8748-bab08de2517c.body:
"In 2021 Kunstmuseum Den Haag organised the exhibition 'Global Wardrobe'. For this project I really wanted to show this design by Rich Mnisi, because it is not only very fashionable but also uses traditional knotting techniques from VaTsonga culture. What is special about this design is that no less than five kilometres of thread went into the skirt. Mnisi only made this garment to order, to avoid overproduction. Kunstmuseum Den Haag ordered one, which is now part of the collection.

The skirt was given the title Xibelani and is made of 100% merino wool. The design uses five kilometres of wool threads in light blue, green and white. These threads are knotted to metal rings attached to this orange belt of 100% nappa leather, which closes with a silver-coloured metal buckle."
be8bf109-5677-4714-8748-bab08de2517c.title: Knotting with 5 kilometres of thread

6d2045f6-ac5f-439d-bc09-19b422b07c90.body:
"Probably worn for military affairs, it is assumed this cape was worn by Ernst Casimir I when visiting troops at the Siege of Roermond in 1632. The garment encompasses everything a leading official should be; it is both practical, yet beautifully constructed using the finest of fabrics.

The top of the cape, around the chest and shoulder, would have been worn quite close to the body as was customary at the time. The garment then flares outwards at the waist, ensuring comfortable and flexibility of movement when riding on horseback."
6d2045f6-ac5f-439d-bc09-19b422b07c90.title: A Practical Garment

bf4dc176-2eb1-4dc5-b156-417b127e11cd.body:
"Can you spot the stitches around each buttonhole? Large silver-gilt threads, wrapped around silk, run vertically at the ends of the horizontal openings. These stitches serve no practical purpose; instead, they signal wealth and high rank, making the officer’s status unmistakable.

At the top of each sleeve, ten pieces of tightly woven wool overlap the sleeve opening. These sections are carefully bound together with the same gleaming silver-gilt threads. The stitches are deliberately large, designed to catch the light and draw attention to the garment’s extravagance."
bf4dc176-2eb1-4dc5-b156-417b127e11cd.title: Shining threads

426154e1-626a-4ef2-92b1-22ac21a6462e.body:
"While researching this highlight of the collection, we came across a unique photo: wide-eyed, little Gerlacus Ribbius Peletier Jr. (1887-1969) poses in this dress on a carte de visite in 1889. ‘Gerlachje’ (little Gerlach) wears it with dark knee socks and smart little shoes.

Gerlach junior was born as the first child and only son of Gerlacus Peletier and Adriana Louise Wijbelingh. He would be the last male bearer of the name in the wealthy Utrecht cigar family."
426154e1-626a-4ef2-92b1-22ac21a6462e.title: Little Gerlach

f07238c8-310d-4f79-9caa-1bf3bbf9cf2f.body:
"How we link certain colours to someone's gender is not fixed. While girls now wear a lot of pink clothes, a little over 100 years ago this colour was actually seen as a typical boys' colour. Men wore pink too, as this elegant suit from around 1770 shows, among other things.

Pink was then seen as a strong and convincing colour, qualities that people at the time thought suited boys more than girls. Blue, on the other hand, was considered softer, like the blue of the Virgin Mary. Who knows where our colour associations will take us in 100 years…"
f07238c8-310d-4f79-9caa-1bf3bbf9cf2f.title: Pink is for...

f22c176d-2925-41c4-af4e-a7e71dce927f.body:
"A white child's dress with smocking and pink bows: today it would quickly be seen as a ‘typical girl's garment’. Until recently, that is also how it was listed in the museum database. But nothing could be further from the truth! This short woollen winter dress was for a two-year-old boy.

From the second half of the sixteenth century until the end of the nineteenth century, it was common to dress both boys and girls in a dress during their first years of life, as can also be seen here with the Prince of Orange."
f22c176d-2925-41c4-af4e-a7e71dce927f.title: A dress for boys

1c1a86fe-ceaa-4e07-8aef-c2459004266e.body: "The lining is made of a pink wool grain fabric. Like the chintz, the lining is calendered, which makes it shiny, firm and dirt-repellent. The use of plain wool grain is typical of Zaan jackets. It is usually in a colour that matches the fabric, but often not. Several bright yellow linings in jackets are known, for example. You sometimes also find them in expensive silk skirts, as seen in this photo."
1c1a86fe-ceaa-4e07-8aef-c2459004266e.title: A durable lining

2048ae26-62ba-4097-8ff3-8587e6ef6c9c.body:
"This pink Empire jacket, as you can tell from the waist and the size, was made for a girl. Old fold and sewing marks in the textile tell us that the jacket was made from another garment. Because the separate elbow pieces have survived, we also know that it comes from an 18th-century woman's jacket and was remade.

It was probably not worn much, because the jacket is in very good condition and its colour is still beautiful. Striking are the very deep neckline and the raised waist. It is a long jacket without a seam at the front. The joining seams all run to the back, so the jacket can no longer be worn over a wide skirt. The side seams and centre back have double box pleats."
2048ae26-62ba-4097-8ff3-8587e6ef6c9c.title: Remade into an Empire jacket for a girl

31619894-aef9-4455-9872-9d7e51efcfc1.body:
"Chintz is a shiny, washable cotton fabric from India that, after a long treatment with mordants, dyes and wax resist, is painted or printed in many colours. In the eighteenth century chintz was also produced in Europe. The fabric of this jacket is European chintz.

On a bright pink ground, exotic little tufts of flowers have been ‘scattered’, as it were, surrounded by light brown circles with black hatching. Pink chintz is rare in the Netherlands. Only one other similar woman's jacket is known, in a private Zaan collection. You come across it only rarely in antique patchwork quilts."
31619894-aef9-4455-9872-9d7e51efcfc1.title: Pink chintz

450f213b-c036-4c3c-8949-0863ed0b3d6c.body:
"The 18th-century jacket that belongs with these, called a kassekien, was remade into an Empire jacket for a girl in the 19th century. Before that, the woman wore these matching little wreaths around the elbows, with lace sleeve ruffles attached. The wreaths were sewn onto the jacket with two stitches when visitors came, and afterwards they had to come off quickly, or the lace would wear. Wreaths as separate elements are typical of Zaan regional dress. The original wreaths have survived.

The type of sleeve we see here on the remade girl's jacket came into fashion around 1790 to 1794. After that it disappeared for a while, and around 1810 it came back into fashion for a longer period. From 1810, the part that falls over the hand was richly decorated. So you can tell from this jacket that whoever wore it did not belong to the working class."
450f213b-c036-4c3c-8949-0863ed0b3d6c.title: With and without little wreaths

64441729-e209-42ad-bd9e-1eceec7493a9.body:
"Thanks to these inventory labels on the inside, we know that this special garment made a remarkable journey through museums, attics and expert hands before it arrived where it is kept now.

This jacket comes from the collection of Cruys Voorbergh, an actor and costume expert. His expertise and carefully restored collection led to the founding of the Netherlands Costume Museum in The Hague. After his death in 1963, his collection was housed in the Haags Gemeentemuseum (now Kunstmuseum Den Haag).

The Kunstmuseum gave the jacket to Museum Marken as ‘Marken dress’. There it lay in the attic for many years, with no one knowing what to do with it. Only in 2023 was it recognised by Adriaantje de Jong, curator of Museum Spakenburg, as a Zaan girl's jacket, and it was given to the Zaans Museum."
64441729-e209-42ad-bd9e-1eceec7493a9.title: Back to the Zaan

2c15fcea-a7c6-40fc-a898-fb060907a718.body:
"Thanks to this wedding portrait, we know when someone was married in this dress. Thursday 14 April 1864 was the big day for Simon van Gijn and Cornelia Agatha Vriesendorp from Dordrecht. On this fresh spring day they said yes to each other. The couple were fashionably dressed that day: in their wedding photo Simon wears a dark tailcoat, while Cornelia wears this white gown with an enormous crinoline. Around her head she has a veil that reaches almost to the ground. She was completely up to date.

Not only their clothes show that the newly married Van Gijn – Vriesendorp couple kept up with the latest developments. They also had themselves photographed on their big day. This only became a common wedding ritual at the end of the 19th century, so the Dordrecht couple can be called pioneers.

Besides fashion, symbolism also plays an important role in this wedding portrait. It is striking that Simon holds one of his gloves in his hand. Taking off the glove can be seen as a symbol of intimacy between husband and wife and the sealing of the marriage. In seventeenth-century portraits, the man offers his wife the glove as a sign of his faithfulness.

Cornelia, whom Simon affectionately called Corretje, died young, in 1889. Van Gijn kept her wedding dress until his death in 1922, when he left it to the museum. It is one of the few personal belongings of Cornelia that have survived.”
2c15fcea-a7c6-40fc-a898-fb060907a718.title: A memory of Corretje

59faef0a-7f61-48fd-8897-c746152ee225.body:
"Judging by the gown, Cornelia had her wedding dress made by an experienced dressmaker, who carefully put the dress together by hand. The bride-to-be chose a cream-coloured moiré rib silk, which is expertly matched at the back. This watered pattern gives the fabric a luxurious look.

 Her high neckline fits perfectly with the bridal fashion of this period, which by then followed the fashion line for afternoon dresses . A low neckline was no longer thought to suit the newly risen ideal of the virtuous woman.

The gown also has a vertical row of small buttons on the chest, wide sleeves and a large hoop skirt. Fashion plates of the time show that Cornelia was very well informed about the latest bridal fashion. Even her long transparent veil, falling around her whole body, is bon ton."
59faef0a-7f61-48fd-8897-c746152ee225.title: Sparkling in moiré

b73291be-77ea-41c8-8830-f0e463de662d.body:
"In the 19th century, the light-coloured wedding dress became more and more popular in higher circles. White was no longer just a fashion colour but was also chosen symbolically as fitting the rite of passage. By marrying, the girl was no longer seen as a child but as a grown woman. White stood for childlike purity and innocence, and with that also virginity.

On her wedding day Cornelia chose more symbolism: sprigs of orange blossom were placed on her waist and in her little crown, a symbol of happiness, purity and fertility. In Corretje's time this was an emerging wedding custom. In the following decades, wearing orange blossom, real or artificial, would become very popular."
b73291be-77ea-41c8-8830-f0e463de662d.title: White and orange blossom: a tradition in the making

f41445bc-aef6-4415-9fe6-f1887bf7b9f7.body:
“This gown was shown in the exhibition Ja, ik wil! (Yes, I do!) at the Fries Museum in Leeuwarden (2024-2025), about the wedding dress over the past 250 years, with historical, modern and contemporary dresses. At its centre is the wedding dress in the Netherlands. The museum takes visitors on a journey through time, from the 18th century to today, in search of the essence of the wedding dress. Which fashions and traditions shaped it? Where does the ‘white’ wedding dress as we know it today come from? And what does the dress say about its wearer?

For each dress there was attention for both the fashion and the wearer. About Cornelia Vriesendorp: ‘Cornelia and Simon probably met at one of the many parties of Dordrecht's small elite. After their wedding they are comfortably off, not least because Simon is a banker and lawyer. ‘Corretje’ loves fashion and goes shopping in Paris and Brussels every year. But no family follows. In 1872 their only son is stillborn.’”
f41445bc-aef6-4415-9fe6-f1887bf7b9f7.title: Bridal fashion in Ja, ik wil!

3d765290-e1fe-4d2b-9a57-ca9d579889e4.body: "Embroidered decorations, home-made or not, have for centuries been a fine way to stand out from the crowd, or to show which group you belong to. Hundreds of messages are hidden in the knotted and stitched threads: where you come from, for example, who your family is or where your loyalties lie. Colours, motifs, patterns and initials connect garments with their wearer, so one's own personality can be expressed in a unique way. In this case, the wearer used it to show that she was extremely rich."
3d765290-e1fe-4d2b-9a57-ca9d579889e4.title: Embroidery makes the person

5d61bca6-ea3c-409d-9ded-6ad982e4c6f3.body:
"These red velvet shoes, embroidered with gold thread and sequins, come from Liauckema State in Sexbierum. This house was one of the largest in Friesland and for centuries belonged to members of the rich and influential Liauckema family.

Given their date of around 1620, Catharina van Liauckema (1592-1656) could have worn the shoes. At that time she lived in Mechelen, where her husband Dierick van der Laen was mayor.

In a portrait from 1622 she shows herself in her finest clothes, displaying a huge variety of precious things: jewellery, lace, fur, embroidery, velvets and woven fabrics. This luxurious footwear with gold thread and velvet certainly fits in with that."
5d61bca6-ea3c-409d-9ded-6ad982e4c6f3.title: Catharina van Liauckema

6c4ed034-e3dc-4cd0-881a-4b1654155719.body:
"Although these velvet shoes with gold thread were probably worn by a woman, they were almost certainly embroidered by a man. Embroiderers, almost exclusively men, were united in a guild that kept a strict eye on the quality of the work.

For example, the metal thread used, a thin rolled strip of gold or silver wound around a linen or silk core, had to contain the right proportion of silver or gold. For these shoes, silver-gilt thread was used, with sequins set between it. It was sewn onto the velvet with small stitches to show as much of the precious thread as possible."
6c4ed034-e3dc-4cd0-881a-4b1654155719.title: Stitch by stitch: a man's job

bf4f42c5-2ec2-46f3-a4e5-9a9c00a9a733.body: "Had the shoes been a few sizes bigger, they could just as well have belonged to Catharina's husband Dierick. In this period men wore the same shoes as women: a short style of leather or velvet with a round toe, a low heel and two straps fastened over the instep. The fastening was hidden under a rosette, which grew larger and larger over the century."
bf4f42c5-2ec2-46f3-a4e5-9a9c00a9a733.title: Women's or men's shoes?

59979a88-9e75-e151-5087-ce6bdcd7a006.body:
"Nel Linssen's design is reminiscent of the millstone ruff, an iconic fashion accessory of the 16th and early 17th centuries. This ‘ruff’ grew into an impressive circular collar of pleated linen, stiffened with starch and sometimes whalebone. It was a status symbol of the nobility, where clothing expressed power and etiquette.

The video shows how such a collar was made: narrow strips of fabric were carefully pleated and starched into a perfectly rhythmic volume. Can you see these techniques in Nel Linssen's paper collar?"
59979a88-9e75-e151-5087-ce6bdcd7a006.title: Millstone ruff

6a5b1c8c-06b2-30c5-f4ba-43f9eca5465f.body: "Nel Linssen started making paper jewellery in the mid-1980s. She carried out countless studies of the technical possibilities and ways of folding she could use to achieve the visual effect or movement she wanted. The circle was the most important shape for her: this geometric form appears most often in her designs. Her background in working with textiles often shows in her designs, and so in this necklace too: because of the way it is folded, it drapes around the neck in an organic, flowing way."
6a5b1c8c-06b2-30c5-f4ba-43f9eca5465f.title: Flowing paper

e442984a-8cdf-7f00-bfa1-44d38dbc5003.body:
“In this video, Nel Linssen herself shows different techniques she uses, such as rhythmic folding, rolling, cutting and sliding pieces into each other. With paper she can create sharp, precise pleats that keep their shape, but also soft waves and curves.

This creates a rich range of possibilities: Linssen uses these craft techniques to make jewellery such as this collar, which looks sculptural yet is light and wearable, a contemporary translation of historical pleated forms such as the millstone ruff."
e442984a-8cdf-7f00-bfa1-44d38dbc5003.title: Folding techniques

604f693b-c0a5-a14d-8a74-99fa3c852d6b.body:
"Mother Roos Jenniskens had to improvise during the textile shortage: her liberation suit is made of different kinds of orange fabric. You can also see this in the pennants that Roos, like the suits, made in secret while waiting for the end of the Second World War. When the British liberators entered Meterik in Limburg in November 1944, these pennants fluttered proudly in the air.

Three of these flags are also in the collection of the Netherlands Open Air Museum. One stands out because it combines white and orange fabric. And that is where the mystery begins: the fabric of the trousers looks very much like the flag fabric. Could the suit and the flags have been made from the same pieces of cloth?"
604f693b-c0a5-a14d-8a74-99fa3c852d6b.title: Textile shortage

6865aa5a-e49c-a419-bfcb-4d0434df963b.body:
"You recognise this sailor collar straight away: flat over the shoulders, ending in a little tie. The V-neck is filled in with a separate bib. For centuries, the sailor look produced timeless, much-loved children's clothing for special occasions. 

Roos Jenniskens clearly knew her fashion classics. In strict secrecy she sewed an orange sailor suit for her little sons Jan and Harrie. She did give both sailors a contemporary ‘remake’, though. Jan wore a ‘schuitje’ or side cap, cheekily tilted on his head.

Like countless cute little boys and girls before them, Jan and his brother had their photo taken in their festive sailor suits. In November 1944 their village of Meterik in Limburg was liberated by the British army."
6865aa5a-e49c-a419-bfcb-4d0434df963b.title: Cute in a sailor look

9af865aa-de3f-53fa-542b-58edb55e4d1e.body: "If you look closely, you can see Jan Jenniskens' elegantly embroidered initials on this orange cap. His mother Roos Jenniskens-Engels could work magic with needle and thread and made all the clothes for her family herself, including this sailor suit. These initials make the personalities of the maker and the wearer, mother and son, tangible."
9af865aa-de3f-53fa-542b-58edb55e4d1e.title: Orange home-made fashion

4235724a-7ca2-d7f4-9041-25ed4ffe1f09.body:
"You can see from this highlight of the collection why designer and artist Fong Leng (1937) is regarded as ‘la grande dame’ of Dutch fashion. With unique creations like this and spectacular fashion shows she became very well known in the 1970s and 1980s.

Fong Leng's fashion shows are remarkable, as is her outspoken approach to her designs as art and not fashion: she did not follow trends and only pursued her own taste. This also resulted in a strikingly outspoken, extravagant style, balancing between art and fashion."
4235724a-7ca2-d7f4-9041-25ed4ffe1f09.title: La Grande Dame

68a65278-18f7-f36d-155e-15b7c07860ff.body:
"As soon as you see the bottom of this coat, it is clear why it is called the ‘leopard coat’. Stylised leopards, applied in leather, creep between coloured grass. Leopards often stand for the strength of a brave warrior and elusive beauty.

Interestingly, a photo turned up in the archive of fashion designer Frank Govers at the Kunstmuseum (he was a friend of the wearer of this coat, Mathilde Willink) that raises questions about a possible source of inspiration. In this very 1970s photo, Mathilde poses in a flamboyant Fong Leng coat of gold leather from 1972 … accompanied by a real leopard. The similarities between this photo and the theme of the leopard coat raise speculation: could this moment have led to the creation of the iconic leopard coat?"
68a65278-18f7-f36d-155e-15b7c07860ff.title: Leopards in the wild

7f117f06-540a-3253-0c06-de3fcab82f69.body:
"Few people know that the hidden inside of the leopard coat has a grey-purple, almost lilac lining. A world away from the golden, glittering outside of the coat.

The lining is edged with red binding. Under the red binding on the right side there is a kind of red-pink stain . The stain seems strategically placed and has a sharp, clearly defined shape. Some speculate that it is a kiss. Is it an ink stain, an accident? Or was Fong Leng trying to tell us something?"
7f117f06-540a-3253-0c06-de3fcab82f69.title: Smudged ink or a secret message?

a9a4bbc1-1567-9787-76e9-55dc4f0bf3d4.body:
"In her work, Fong Leng often found inspiration in her Chinese roots. This ranges from East Asian printmaking and elements of architecture to colours and shapes from different art styles. The design of this leopard in a swamp landscape gives an impression of this artistic translation."

Fong Leng: "As an artist I have never denied my Chinese background; I always try to bring my roots to the surface. Just try mixing the Chinese with the Dutch. Sometimes I am torn. That also makes it interesting, because I don't know what will come out." - Quote from 'Meer dan Babi Pangang', 2020.
a9a4bbc1-1567-9787-76e9-55dc4f0bf3d4.title: Chinese inspiration

bf4fb8bb-b8ec-072a-0986-b47af7288670.body: "They are hard to miss: the three-dimensional rosettes of gold and silver leather on the shoulders and sleeves of the Leopard Coat. Applying the flowers is one of Fong Leng's signature techniques: leatherwork and appliqué. Fong Leng also prefers to 'paint' in her favourite material: leather. The appliqués add a detailed dimension to an already striking design."
bf4fb8bb-b8ec-072a-0986-b47af7288670.title: Creating with leather

f9ede90e-ec12-11d7-5434-f65757db565a.body:
"Mathilde Willink (1938-1977), who wore this coat, was Fong Leng's best-known client and friend. She was given the coat by her husband Carel Willink (1900-1983).

She was often seen in this creation on the streets of Amsterdam. Under the coat Mathilde wore only short ruffled shorts. At 1.90 metres tall and dressed in Fong Leng's designs, she was a striking figure whose photos often appeared in the press. Other women bought extreme pieces like this from Fong Leng too, but the difference with Mathilde was that she had racks full of them. She did not just walk around in them, she lived in them.

Willink portrayed Mathilde several times. In 1975, when their relationship was ending, he painted her full-length in the coat. He gave the work the title 'Farewell to Mathilde'. After Mathilde's death in 1979, the leopard coat was auctioned at Sotheby Mak van Waay, where the Amsterdam (Historical) Museum bought it."
f9ede90e-ec12-11d7-5434-f65757db565a.title: Farewell to Mathilde

0094a082-0868-45d2-aa74-d464403b9009.body:
On the waist stay inside the jacket, ‘Mme. J. (De) Terlinge(n) - Utrecht’ is printed in gold letters. Around 1879 this studio for ‘Robes et Costumes’ was based in Utrecht, run by Madame J. (De) Terlinge(n). Unfortunately, little else is known about her. It is the oldest Utrecht fashion label in the collection of the Centraal Museum. The waist stays also keep the jacket firmly in place while it is worn.

From the mid-1860s more garments were ‘signed’, including by Madame Roger, Pingat and the fashion designer and visionary Charles Frederick Worth (1825-1895), the founder of haute couture.
0094a082-0868-45d2-aa74-d464403b9009.title: Signed

357503a7-76ab-46b8-b747-926fb1172362.body:
This black gown from 1879 marks a transitional period in fashion. The high-necked jacket and the long, close-fitting sleeves fit the style of 1870-1878. The ruffles and smocking in the skirt are also typical of this time.

The length of the fitted jacket, on the other hand, was new, as was the tournure or queue de Paris: the name for the structure that creates volume on the inside of the back of the skirt. The length of the skirt was new too: both the front of the skirt and the train at the back only just miss the ground. This new fashion was a first step towards more freedom of movement for women.
357503a7-76ab-46b8-b747-926fb1172362.title: Transitional fashion

b741d54b-d2e5-4503-bb33-0e8ae0c1874d.body:
Presenting historical garments is precision work that takes a lot of research, attention and time. This gown has been dressed on a polypropylene foam torso, cut to the right silhouette and padded with fibrefill where needed. Over that goes a home-made jersey cover , with a fabric-covered cardboard disc at the neck.

Underwear from this period usually consisted of a petticoat, a corset and a small cushion or a boned tournure (bustle). For this mounting, other means were used to create the desired silhouette: a straight back, narrow waist, sloping shoulders and a monobosom. Here that was achieved with a wide, gathered cotton petticoat and a cushion suggesting the shape of the tournure.

Original historical underwear is preferably not used. These pieces are often very fragile and can lose their shape or be damaged when under tension for a long time. That is why modern materials are usually used to create the right silhouette, and the historical objects stay safely preserved in the store.
b741d54b-d2e5-4503-bb33-0e8ae0c1874d.title: Made-to-measure mounting

d02a8957-f8a5-46b9-b173-7a2140db39c4.body:
Black may not be the first colour that comes to mind for a festive occasion like a wedding. Yet we know for certain that this gown was worn on 23 December 1879 by Johanna Frederika Maria de Greve (1852-1903) when she married Henri François Wouter Dubois (1844-1932). The main reason is that her father had just died, which makes it a mourning gown as well. Black was also a popular fashion colour in the late 19th century. For a long time, people married in their most beautiful coloured dress, which could also be worn after the festivities.

Marrying in white gradually came in from around 1820. The white lace edges at the neck and cuffs of the jacket do create a contrast with the black, together with the white gloves with fine black buttons and the bridal hair wreath with two black ribbons that serve as a fastening.
d02a8957-f8a5-46b9-b173-7a2140db39c4.title: Married in black?

91a1b874-c7b2-4a86-9480-e17328ebd560.body:
"In the nineteenth century, fancy-dress parties were held very widely, both indoors and outdoors. The elite entertained themselves at private parties and at court. In private circles, tableaux vivants were staged to amuse guests.

Guests invited to a fancy-dress party had a costume made or used old clothes from the family. Like this brown silk gown with leg-of-mutton sleeves (c. 1836), which was worn again in a tableau vivant in 1889 to celebrate the wedding of the Dordrecht couple Vriesendorp-Roodenburg. The scene shown in the photo is the 'gilding party' described in Hildebrand's book Camera Obscura. Can you spot the gown in the photo?"
91a1b874-c7b2-4a86-9480-e17328ebd560.title: Tableaux vivants

c6896988-042f-a8bf-ce78-c1635e825eda.body:
"During preparations for the exhibition Slow Fashion (2019), these two gowns were examined closely. That led to an unexpected discovery: they are made from the same sturdy, probably eighteenth-century piece of fabric!

This is shown, among other things, by the selvages (reinforced woven edges) of the fabric and the provenance. Both gowns come from the Den Bandt family. The connection had never been made before, because the garments entered the collection decades apart. On top of that, one gown is lighter in colour. This, however, is fading caused by the gown having been on display for too long in the past."
c6896988-042f-a8bf-ce78-c1635e825eda.title: A pair reunited

c8ba87df-adb8-4370-8ed6-87178f630922.body:
"Under the influence of Romanticism, the fashionable silhouette for women changed from 1825. Women had a tightly laced waist, full skirts, broad shoulders and wide sleeves. The broad shoulders and large leg-of-mutton sleeves were inspired by the sleeve of sixteenth-century men's dress.

To create the desired volume, ladies wore sleeve puffers. These little cushions were worn loose or attached to the corset. The leg-of-mutton sleeves reached their maximum volume in 1830. From the 1830s, the leg-of-mutton sleeve stayed fashionable but shrank in volume and proportions."
c8ba87df-adb8-4370-8ed6-87178f630922.title: Leg-of-mutton sleeves

0d42d66f-2e16-de04-70ce-5f96ee1ef367.body: "The cocoons in Chequita Nahar's piece refer to the cocoons of the silkworm. In this video you can see how a silkworm makes them."
0d42d66f-2e16-de04-70ce-5f96ee1ef367.title: Cocoon

45325f87-ae9b-69ee-429e-3accb3e9a705.body:
"Chequita Nahar (Paramaribo, 1970) is a Dutch jewellery designer, teacher and curator. Her work comes from her bicultural background and is a fusion of different cultural influences. In her jewellery she combines Surinamese crafts and techniques with methods from contemporary jewellery practice.

In this video from AVRO Kunstuur, Nahar talks openly about her work, alternating with jewellery designer Uli Rapp, who in turn shares her own story."
45325f87-ae9b-69ee-429e-3accb3e9a705.title: Chequita Nahar

14c0fa89-ef4c-4ba1-a12d-99acd2364e78.body:
"Hannah de Vries wore a Beatles dress as a teenager. “I got the dress in 1964, the year the Beatles came to the Netherlands, when I was about thirteen or fourteen and in my second year of secondary school. I really wanted the dress, because I thought The Beatles were fantastic. It was the first time I was really a fan of music. They made such great songs.”

“Lots of girls in my class had a Beatles dress, but it wasn't something you wore to school every day. It was more of a statement. I wore it now and then, sometimes after school; then my friends put theirs on too and we played Beatles music together.”

 “I think I wore it for a year, because your figure changes in your teens. When you're fifteen you don't wear something like that any more, at least I didn't. It was a bit of a sack dress, really.”"
14c0fa89-ef4c-4ba1-a12d-99acd2364e78.title: The Beatles in the Netherlands

7dededb5-c9cb-4309-94f7-9c74dc6ce9c2.body:
"Hannah de Vries's Beatles dress was made for her by her mother. “She was incredibly handy and often made clothes for me and my little brother. But that was still quite normal back then anyway.”

 Mother and daughter bought the fabric in a fabric shop in Nijmegen. “The fabric was sold on the roll, but you couldn't just buy half a metre of it,” says Hannah. “You bought the fabric by the panel: two pieces, one for the front of the dress and one for the back. Two panels together cost ten guilders. The idea was that you made an A-line dress from them. Everyone wore that kind of dress at the time. My mother said: don't get pink or light blue, so I got beige. I did think it was short. Even at thirteen I was quite tall for my age. Other people thought so too: that the dress was on the short side .”

 “You could also buy the Beatles dresses ready-made in the shop, at C&A,” Hannah remembers. “They were more expensive there: twelve guilders fifty. But they were made less nicely. A C&A dress was for girls whose mothers couldn't sew, or mothers who worked and weren't at home.”
7dededb5-c9cb-4309-94f7-9c74dc6ce9c2.title: Home-made or shop-bought

901d5ae0-6108-44ab-a4d2-c3834b8d5005.body: "Who wouldn't want one: a ‘signed’ dress with your favourite band on it? In 1964 Stoomweverij Nijverheid in Enschede bought the rights to produce cotton ‘Beatles fabric’ in different designs and colours. You can see the Fab Four and their signatures in a contemporary Op Art design. In-house designer Henny Hoogenboom drew these portraits of John, Paul, George and Ringo from official Beatles photos. For fashion-conscious Beatles fans of the time, undoubtedly a must-have."
901d5ae0-6108-44ab-a4d2-c3834b8d5005.title: Yeah-Yeah dress

ea4e5eef-7a30-4f1e-91fa-ee744df4847d.body: "Up close you can see the simple fit of this mini dress. Besides ready-made Beatles dresses, a sew-it-yourself pattern was also for sale. For just fl. 9.90 you received two pattern pieces printed to shape, with only two diagonal darts. A straightforward dress in two halves: ideal for the not-so-experienced seamstress with little patience. This wearer, too, sewed her shift dress together a little sloppily. How ‘mini’ would she have worn this dress? You could easily decide that with your own scissors."
ea4e5eef-7a30-4f1e-91fa-ee744df4847d.title: A simple cut

b54f8b8d-3ba1-4c71-bf6c-377fc8a87509.body:
"How does this cap get its shape? In this film, Aaf Steur-Sombroek shows how a Volendam hul is made up.

The hul is cleaned, dried and treated with starch, dried again, treated with starch again, rolled in a cloth and ironed. Then the pleats are put in, ironed and pinned to pleat, the pleating is tacked in place and regularly coated with starch again. This sometimes takes 2 or 3 days. It is an extremely labour-intensive process."
b54f8b8d-3ba1-4c71-bf6c-377fc8a87509.title: Stiffly pleated

2ea8d77c-45bc-4df1-b35f-272a3f87e14e.body:
"The square shoulder scarf was folded diagonally and pleated along the long side. The pattern of the fabric was different for boys and girls, to make the difference clear.

Boys in skirts wore flowered shoulder scarves. For girls, checked fabric was used. This one is made of a piece of printed cotton. For special occasions, people preferred scarves with a border motif."
2ea8d77c-45bc-4df1-b35f-272a3f87e14e.title: Flowers versus checks

36442afe-de56-452a-a304-6180f3ca2326.body:
"Can you see the difference between this sleeve and the one on the jacket in the extra photo?

In skirt dress, the sleeves of a jacket differed for boys and girls. Girls' sleeves closed with hooks and eyes, while boys' sleeves had a cuff at the bottom closed with a silver button. The size and style of that button depended on personal taste, wealth and the occasion."
36442afe-de56-452a-a304-6180f3ca2326.title: A boy's sleeve

7acf8658-ee4b-4eb1-84f2-b3875cc93711.body:
"Can you see this tuck here? It is there for a reason.

Aprons were made with room to grow. A new apron was always a little too long, so the fabric at the bottom was sewn double for a short stretch. As the child grew, you let out this tuck ."
7acf8658-ee4b-4eb1-84f2-b3875cc93711.title: Room to grow

bc7fe521-b337-4bd1-9450-faf78632234d.body:
"This combination could have been worn in the middle of the 20th century by a boy from Rouveen, in the municipality of Staphorst. In Staphorst and Rouveen, boys wore skirts from their baptism until about their third year. This was not unique to these villages but was found in many regional dresses. In general fashion, too, it was once normal for little boys to wear a skirt or dress. By the 1960s, boys in skirts had disappeared from the streets of Staphorst and Rouveen.

This costume is part of the regional dress collection brought together by the Stichting Nederlandse Volksklederdrachten ‘Collectie Koningin Wilhelmina’ (Foundation for Dutch Folk Costume ‘Queen Wilhelmina Collection’, Stichting HM). The collection is owned by the Royal Collections and managed by the Netherlands Open Air Museum.

The basis for this ensemble was put together in 1953 at the request of Stichting HM, by a contact person from Rouveen. For this 360-degree photo, the set was completed with a shirt and a collar stud from the national collection. The costume has often been shown in exhibitions and, if you look closely at the fabric, it is therefore somewhat faded."
bc7fe521-b337-4bd1-9450-faf78632234d.title: Layers put together

c19a18eb-cf8d-4a96-81ea-1339a4831c30.body: "On his first birthday a boy got his first collar stud: two buttons of silver or gold joined by a ring. From that day on he wore it every day to close his shirt collar. The first collar stud was often a gift from the grandfather the boy was named after. Most boys first wore a silver one, which was replaced by a gold one when they were older. Boys from wealthy farming families got a gold collar stud straight away. Here we see a silver collar stud."
c19a18eb-cf8d-4a96-81ea-1339a4831c30.title: Collar studs

ed7baa17-1e34-4c0c-9283-465d306fa304.body: "A toddler's apron had a so-called ‘slamiere’ at the top: a waistband with two shoulder straps. The slamiere of this apron is made of colourful checked cotton, with a different fabric on the inside, so an apron like this could be worn on both sides. The toddler's apron was the same for boys and girls."
ed7baa17-1e34-4c0c-9283-465d306fa304.title: Wearable both ways

04a95448-3add-4c7c-9a60-657c779a2373.body: "In the upper circles of 18th-century Friesland, English or French fashion mixed with local touches. In this wedding costume, for example, the fashionable wide gown with a tight bodice has been translated into the typically Frisian jacket and skirt. The accessories, a matching frame bag and a gold ear iron over a striking ‘Duitse’ (dietsche) cap, give the costume a strong Frisian touch."
04a95448-3add-4c7c-9a60-657c779a2373.title: Fashion in Friesland

0ec3e3b4-3eaf-4cbd-bd89-2ff8ca7a7bf0.body:
“It was a special experience: parading digitally in Isabella's wedding dress in the Modemuze AR fitting mirror. For a moment I felt what it must have been like to walk, turn and even dance in such a stately dress with wide hips. The dress, and her story, came to life.

For the exhibition Ja, ik wil! (Yes, I do!, 2024) we digitised a number of wedding dresses from the Fries Museum in 3D together with Tijdlab. This was technically complex: transparent and shiny fabrics were a challenge for 3D scanning, a technique that is developing at a rapid pace. Accessories such as the cap, the apron and the mitts were therefore removed temporarily.

With 360-degree photography and photogrammetry we built a movable 3D model, optimised for our digital mirror. This let visitors imagine themselves for a moment in the shoes of a bride from the past. In this way we bring heritage even closer to the public: not only by looking, but by experiencing it themselves without damaging the museum objects."
0ec3e3b4-3eaf-4cbd-bd89-2ff8ca7a7bf0.title: Wearing it digitally

c3df5732-4701-427a-ba7f-1511d44a7fed.body:
"At the beginning of the eighteenth century, women began wearing a neckerchief of thin, transparent fabric to cover the low-cut neckline of their jackets and gowns. The square neckerchief, or fichu, worn with the point (tip) on the back, was called a tipdoek in Friesland.

White embroidery (whitework) was used to try to imitate expensive lace. Point de Saxe, the delicate embroidery that decorates this tipdoek, can hardly be told apart from lace at a distance because of the fine holes of the openwork. The holes are made by pulling the stitches tight, not, as in other techniques, by drawing out threads. This technique can produce a huge variety of patterns to fill the different areas. Using threads of different thicknesses also gives the fabric texture and creates shadow effects."

* This fichu dates from around 1750 and did not belong to Isabella Stinstra, but she will have worn something similar
c3df5732-4701-427a-ba7f-1511d44a7fed.title: A tipdoek with whitework

db79abab-e2ef-4388-b104-f106c12fa2d1.body:
“To give this very wide skirt the right broad silhouette, several mounting techniques were tried. In the first set-ups, the dress form was dressed in several cotton skirts on top of each other with hip pads of Fibrefill (stuffing fibre). The skirt has to be flat at the back, which was hard to achieve with this method; the shape quickly became too round. In a next experiment, a custom-cut sheet of Etafoam (polyethylene foam) was used with a ‘petticoat’ of plastic foam. This gave a better result, but still wasn't good enough.

Only when there was more time to make a ‘real’ panier of strong cotton with metal bones, from a pattern in the book Patterns of Fashion no. 5 (The School of Historical Dress), did mounting this costume become much easier. The existing pattern did have to be adapted for Isabella's skirt: the panier was made a lot smaller, as Frisian fashion was a little more restrained than English fashion. Now that we can mount the skirt with a panier, the pleats fall perfectly and the hem of the skirt is nicely parallel to the floor.”
db79abab-e2ef-4388-b104-f106c12fa2d1.title: Made-to-measure paniers

dc309510-6aef-4915-a695-48a740e64a08.body:
"Isabella Stinstra, from a distinguished family in Harlingen, married Pieter, an extremely rich Amsterdam merchant, in this costume. As was customary, the ceremony took place in the bride's home town, and with her bridal clothes Isabella emphasised her Frisian identity.

The couple moved to the Keizersgracht in Amsterdam, where Isabella raised the family. Isabella also quickly shook off her Frisian feathers, as the family portrait from eight years later shows."
dc309510-6aef-4915-a695-48a740e64a08.title: Isabella Stinstra: from Harlingen to Amsterdam

e4b403f1-8641-462a-9b28-9fb48072558a.body:
"With her wedding costume, Isabella wears an impressive Duitse muts (‘Dutch cap’). The ‘Duits’ refers to ‘dietsch’, meaning ‘of the people’. The Duitse muts developed from a more modest canopy cap: a cap with a strip of bobbin lace at the front. Over the years this lace border became bigger and bigger and had to be kept in shape by a metal frame.

For protection against the sun, a straw sun hat could be worn over the cap. A ribbon attached to the hat with little hooks keeps it from blowing away. The Duitse muts was at its biggest around the time of Isabella's wedding in 1782. After that, fashion changed, and in the course of the 19th century it was replaced by the floddermuts."
e4b403f1-8641-462a-9b28-9fb48072558a.title: Big, bigger, biggest: the Duitse muts

ec1b2467-5815-45a1-b43b-08c3832c56e0.body:
"The gold frame bag is made of the same precious striped shot silk as the wedding costume, with a lining of blue-and-white striped fabric.

The gold frame was made by Hendrik Dauw, a German-born silversmith working in Leeuwarden. Inside and out, the frame is richly engraved with whimsical rocailles (shell motifs) and an image of Diana, goddess of the hunt."
ec1b2467-5815-45a1-b43b-08c3832c56e0.title: A frame bag with gold

605ff22d-87f2-420d-b8ac-3b3ca4153f3c.body:
"At first sight they look like delicate leaves, but look again: they are made of thin plastic.

Wiebke Pandikow works with everyday materials such as plastic bags and wood, but gives them a surprising new meaning through a craft-based way of working . In this video she shows how she uses an iron and a soldering iron to transform see-through plastic bags, often from the supermarket, into fragile jewellery."
605ff22d-87f2-420d-b8ac-3b3ca4153f3c.title: Ironing plastic bags

d4396b19-4b59-4d22-b2a1-db313d0edfa1.body:
"This work from Wiebke Pandikow's ‘Herbarium’ collection is a response to plastic consumption in our world. Both our oceans and our bodies are slowly being taken over by plastic. How do we deal with that, and how do we reuse the materials? Every work by Wiebke Pandikow is a poetic translation of these present-day questions. Pandikow's poem about the collection":

"It took millennia for oil to form from dead organic material.
It takes energy and time to make a plastic bag.
And often, mere minutes to discard it.
The life which became the oil, some of which became the bag, is still in there somewhere.
I find it, bring it out, display it. To show you:
there is more here than you thought there was."
d4396b19-4b59-4d22-b2a1-db313d0edfa1.title: Plastic consumption

7f1f3828-3e7c-49ef-9a93-7e2d084b9c23.body:
"After landing, the secret agent has to take off the jump suit as quickly as possible to get to safety. For this, two long zips run from the neck to the ankles. In one smooth movement the wearer can let the suit drop off. This gave it the nickname ‘striptease suit’. 

Under the jump suit the secret agent wears ‘ordinary’ civilian clothes, so he or she can blend in among people unnoticed."
7f1f3828-3e7c-49ef-9a93-7e2d084b9c23.title: A lightning-fast ‘striptease’

ee34ee69-25db-489a-6ee9-ed8dae9115ca.body:
"Just like the gadgets of secret agents in films, the jump suit is full of clever and practical tricks. As workwear it is functional through and through. Can you tell from its shape what this pocket is for?

Everything the secret agent might need is stored in specially shaped pockets reachable from the inside or outside, and in compartments. From a folding spade to bury the suit to a special knife for cutting tangled parachute lines. But also a fighting knife and pistol for self-defence, and even a lethal pill so as not to fall into enemy hands alive if arrested…"
ee34ee69-25db-489a-6ee9-ed8dae9115ca.title: Form follows function

efaa57e8-0d95-8f2e-11ab-1fd88a8050c8.body:
"Not only was the suit specially designed for secret service agents, the camouflage pattern is unique too.

The design, with large blotchy shapes in shades of green and red-brown, was printed by hand on the windproof khaki fabric. Even within this pattern there are differences, because the base fabric did not always have the same colour, and neither did the batches of dye.

This is especially visible here in the clearly different left sleeve. The fabric probably came from a different roll."
efaa57e8-0d95-8f2e-11ab-1fd88a8050c8.title: Unique camouflage

2733012e-d366-3782-3aa8-b36d2788a4dd.body:
“The fabric gives us a hint about the date of this koto. This fabric was especially fashionable around 1900: flowers in vertical rows, alternating with geometric stripes in red and white. 

The pattern of the fabric the koto is made from can also tell something to those who know how to read it. Women bought fabrics in shops or at the market, and could give them a name if they wanted to. Over time everyone knew that name and its meaning. It could refer to the woman's state of mind, or to a personal or local event.

Suriname had no textile manufacturers of its own, and people bought their fabrics in shops in Paramaribo, which imported machine-printed fabrics from Europe and Japan, among other places.”
2733012e-d366-3782-3aa8-b36d2788a4dd.title: A hint in the print

35be5120-b097-acea-4447-017bc3446fb5.body: “The whole ensemble has the same name as the skirt, the koto. Where this name comes from is not entirely clear; it may be derived from cotton. The long skirt is the most important part of the koto and determines the look of the whole ensemble. The skirt must have a lot of volume and be starched and ironed, practically without creases."
35be5120-b097-acea-4447-017bc3446fb5.title: Koto (skirt)

430360d1-07e3-09a3-ec38-2b441bb4c39d.body: "Countless secret messages are hidden in the koto. The way the ribbons hanging on the back of the yaki are worn, for example, tells you about the woman's marital status. Two loose ribbons mean that the woman is unmarried. If they are partly tied, she is in a relationship."
430360d1-07e3-09a3-ec38-2b441bb4c39d.title: Hidden message

865a3883-2e2d-31e9-6231-13f18b6d4cfd.body:
“The koto style consists of a shirt with a jacket and skirt. The visible, loose-fitting white cotton shirt, the empi, is often decorated with embroidery or lace. Over it, above the skirt (the koto), a jacket is always worn, called the yaki or jaki . The two ribbons on the back say something about the wearer's relationship status.

The jacket, the koto and the angisa can all be made from the same fabric, called (h)eristel. Here you can see that the angisa is made from a different fabric.”
865a3883-2e2d-31e9-6231-13f18b6d4cfd.title: Yaki

977494f6-08d3-716a-32ad-20c4481d1993.body:
“If you look closely, you can see a small piece of yellowed paper sticking out of the folds of the angisa. This is a Surinamese newspaper, used to stiffen the angisa so that it kept its shape.

When we studied this angisa in the museum store, we found out that the newspaper is from 1906, which tells us roughly when the angisa was starched into its current shape. A find like this really brings a garment to life.”
977494f6-08d3-716a-32ad-20c4481d1993.title: A scrap of newspaper

a56c6713-bb2d-aca2-e1ef-5c2605298c47.body:
"At the back, too, the koto stands out wide. In this style that comes from the koi or famiri, a padded back roll worn as part of the Bigi koto, the large formal koto. Because of this roll and any extra petticoats, the skirt of the kotomisi stands out further, so the jacket hanging over it also flares out more.

Volume is central to the koto style, and in African cultures, among others, it is also a sign of wealth and status. It is thought to be inspired by the cul de Paris, a kind of padded belt that made the hips or bottom look wider in European fashion of the 18th and 19th centuries."
a56c6713-bb2d-aca2-e1ef-5c2605298c47.title: A koi or famiri for volume

b829b670-1b35-10eb-9018-cc8abf796269.body:
"Angisas are cotton, machine-printed and starched headscarves. With these headdresses, Creole Surinamese women pass on messages through different folding techniques, the pattern, the colour and sometimes the name of the cloth. The meaning they communicate can only be ‘read’ by people who know the language of the angisa.

This angisa is unique and innovative because it combines two different ways of tying: Feda Tere Angisa. The two points of this angisa are folded upwards, a sign that the wearer wanted to show her anger."
b829b670-1b35-10eb-9018-cc8abf796269.title: The language of the angisa

c7949407-0ff0-daae-da4b-754f3ecd65b3.body:
“Many kotos have a kotobere, a large pleat around the waist, in which the extra length of the skirt is tucked away. There is an open seam at the front.

Can you also see an opening in this kotobere? It is there for a reason: women used this opening as a pouch to carry personal belongings, such as money.”
c7949407-0ff0-daae-da4b-754f3ecd65b3.title: Kotobere

cecfc65b-c466-46b5-b63b-bd7b4fe279e9.body:
“Research shows that the koto came about through all kinds of different influences and that enslaved Afro-Creole women developed a style of their own . As in this object, you can see personal style in the embroidered blouse and the folded headscarf.

“There is still a lot of uncertainty about the exact origin of the koto. Books from the 17th and 18th centuries keep repeating that a plantation owner's wife invented the koto to cover the bare bodies of her enslaved female servants, so that her (white) husband would not be tempted. This story is persistent, even in more recent publications, but it is unknown where the information comes from.”
cecfc65b-c466-46b5-b63b-bd7b4fe279e9.title: How the koto developed

4ff65a8a-bc0e-461f-ba1d-cdc56be3046e.body:
"Silk and metal, as seen here, are a combination as spectacular as it is fragile. In the late 19th century, silk was often weighted with metal salts to raise the value of the fabric, because the price was then set by weight instead of by the metre. Weighted silk also gave a gown extra volume, as can be seen in this elegant design by Mme Van der Taelen from the collection, which still radiates craftsmanship and quality.

Now, more than a hundred years later, the consequences are visible: this gown has become very fragile, and the small tears in the fabric will only increase. Sadly, this process cannot be reversed, so restoration is impossible. That makes the ‘rebirth’ of this object in Iris van Herpen's digital 360-degree version all the more interesting, in case it should also tear in the future."
4ff65a8a-bc0e-461f-ba1d-cdc56be3046e.title: A fragile combination

818bd8f8-d642-41f0-ab7b-4d176989b161.body: "Iris van Herpen's designs are often innovative and experimental. She made her international breakthrough with her 3D-printed designs, a technique she has kept refining over the years. Sometimes her designs look like sculptures, yet they have all been worn by models and by many celebrities. "Wearing clothes can be a very exciting and creative form of self-expression", says the designer."
818bd8f8-d642-41f0-ab7b-4d176989b161.title: Wearable sculptures?

fb5ed3a7-b422-46ff-bfb0-825449f79e1a.body:
"“The addiction of constantly escaping reality into digital entertainment is something that is an important part of everyone's world today”, is how Iris van Herpen describes the inspiration for her 2011 Escapism collection.

Craftsmanship and innovation come together in futuristic designs like this dress. With her research into the craft of the future , Van Herpen is taking fashion in a new direction. For her Escapism collection she had metal wire woven into silk. The resulting material can be modelled like a sculpture, which in this case is reminiscent of coral."
fb5ed3a7-b422-46ff-bfb0-825449f79e1a.title: Futuristic coral

33759c12-928b-4108-9ad5-e3ccfc154bef.body:
"Hands are a recurring element in Oppenheim's work. In this design for a belt they play with touch, physicality and alienation. They fold around the body like an embrace, but crossed, they also form a clear barrier to everything coming from outside.

In Surrealism, hands often had an ambiguous meaning: they stand for desire, control, tenderness and violence. Oppenheim plays with that ambivalence. Instead of passive decoration, the body is approached actively. It is embraced, protected, or actually enclosed. In this way she shows physicality as something layered and complex."
33759c12-928b-4108-9ad5-e3ccfc154bef.title: Surrealist hands

dbd6f3fc-3182-4466-930a-d9dfb8e247e6.body:
"Looking at this piece of jewellery, can you tell who made it?

This piece by Meret Oppenheim was made in 2003. She had designed it as early as 1937–1938, but never made it herself. The fact that it was only made decades later, and based on her sketches, raises intriguing questions about authorship.

Although Oppenheim did not make the work with her own hands, the artistic intention is entirely hers. The designs were so detailed and well thought out that the later execution follows her vision closely. So the authorship still lies with Oppenheim: the idea and the form are unmistakably hers. In this way her artistry lives on, even after her death."
dbd6f3fc-3182-4466-930a-d9dfb8e247e6.title: Authorship

1d41671e-4c91-4ec5-814a-772dc12bc29f.body: "In 2014 fashion designer Claes Iversen (1977) presented this grey dress to the public, together with seven other creations. Like precious museum pieces, the models, wrapped in the designs, were presented in wooden crates filled with wood wool. Together, the 8 pieces of this collection formed an ode to couture centred on Iversen's love of craftsmanship and handwork, with many labour-intensive details. "
1d41671e-4c91-4ec5-814a-772dc12bc29f.title: 8 pieces

95b93d72-1206-411f-b41c-ce74cf2ad143.body:
"For centuries people have embroidered with threads of cotton or silk, for example. For extra shine, relief or luxury, designs can be enriched with materials such as beads, pearls and sequins. Iversen did not stay within these existing, classic limits and chose to combine traditional elements with unusual materials. Crystals, beads and rhinestones are embroidered on the fabric of the dress alongside laser-cut perspex plates and metal objects such as keys, little scissors, car body rings, eye screws and thumb screws.  Like a collage, the different objects have been carefully brought together on the bodice. They fan out into the skirt, where the different parts form a kind of geometric flowers.  

The construction hardware refers to the importance Iversen places on construction and craftsmanship. Stripped of their everyday practical function, the items have been turned into a symbol. At the same time, the seemingly simple hardware works as aesthetic decoration, combined with more classic materials. In this grey creation Iversen shows that embroidery is not bound by rules but can be as free as the imagination of the maker and designer allows."
95b93d72-1206-411f-b41c-ce74cf2ad143.title: Embroidering with hardware

c0bf6bf6-022a-499b-b113-c46cc55058c6.body:
"The full skirts of the 1950s were a source of inspiration for the silhouette of the dress. Embroidery plays the leading role in this strapless dress with coarse pleating. The whole bodice is covered in a wealth of labour-intensive decoration, making it an inseparable part of the design. 

A love of old techniques and crafts runs through Claes Iversen's work and keeps returning in his creations. ‘I love everyday, homespun techniques. Just the basics, and using them in a new way’, Iversen said in July 2020."
c0bf6bf6-022a-499b-b113-c46cc55058c6.title: Inspired by the fifties

1aefbf88-fa12-41ac-aa28-c1ac1bc79701.body:
"The ensemble from the patchwork collection was shown in the fashion exhibition Maison Amsterdam in De Nieuwe Kerk, a collaboration between the Amsterdam Museum and the Hermitage Amsterdam (now: H’ART Museum). The ensemble was then acquired for the Amsterdam Museum's collection.

The acquisition then led to the exhibition project Continue This Thread: Karim Adduchi x Tess van Zalinge (2023), in which fashion designer Tess van Zalinge was invited as co-curator to put together an exhibition about the meaning and power of handcraft techniques in contemporary fashion."
1aefbf88-fa12-41ac-aa28-c1ac1bc79701.title: Continue This Thread

d45e2d3c-9a92-4280-8a85-918060a63e26.body:
"The patchwork collection (2020) was born from a need for craft during the uncertain times of the coronavirus pandemic. Here Tess van Zalinge shows her deep interest in the historical techniques of Dutch regional dress, and her drive to innovate and experiment. 

Tess built the collection from leftover materials in her Amsterdam studio. The patchwork of the post-war Liberation Skirt was an important source of inspiration. Van Zalinge studied at the Amsterdam Fashion Institute and designs on the border between couture and ready-to-wear , with a lot of attention to craftsmanship, form, sustainability and femininity."

‘The technique is distinctive, deliberate and individualistic, but for me it also stands for celebration and liberation. The looks celebrate the uniform and show that working with what you have to hand leads to inspiration, innovation and sustainability’, says Tess van Zalinge."
d45e2d3c-9a92-4280-8a85-918060a63e26.title: Inspiration, innovation and sustainability

4a1fe5c9-5f04-49c9-b4b2-fbd0c3d35676.body: "Around his waist the Marken man wears a so-called ‘gezondheid’ (literally ‘health’). This garment is made of red baize, a fulled wool fabric. A gezondheid consists of a back panel, two shoulder panels and two shoulder straps crossed at the back. In several places around the former Zuiderzee, the gezondheid was part of men's dress. It gave the wearer support and kept the lower back and belly warm. Some have the owner's initials embroidered on them."
4a1fe5c9-5f04-49c9-b4b2-fbd0c3d35676.title: The ‘gezondheid’

5b11e6c8-f4fc-4a96-9074-953a6256a8c6.body:
"This is a costume for a Marken man in weekday summer dress, from around 1950. Some of the boys and men of Marken worked in fishing and there were a few farmers on the island. These clothes could be worn on board, for example, for work around the house or on the farm. The museum put this costume together from original objects of different origins.

Costume expert Jan Duyvetter (1915-1985), also an author and illustrator, worked at the Netherlands Open Air Museum in Arnhem from 1947, from 1958 as head of the Costume department. He illustrated a series of prints to document Dutch regional dress, including this everyday summer dress for the Marken man."
5b11e6c8-f4fc-4a96-9074-953a6256a8c6.title: Summer dress for working in

77a91020-966e-4668-8aba-b95827085008.body: "In the summer months, boys and men on Marken swapped their black wool trousers on weekdays for a pair of white linen or cotton. The cut of these summer trousers is the same as that of the regular trousers. Marken trousers have no fly or flap closure: the two front panels overlap a little when worn, so the opening falls closed. The pattern pieces sometimes consist of different pieces of fabric, and the much-used pairs are often patched, of which this seam on the trouser leg is a visible example."
77a91020-966e-4668-8aba-b95827085008.title: Pattern pieces for summer trousers

b3792374-f30b-4ff4-b77f-c40e0964b01e.body:
"Over their underclothes, Marken boys and men wore a so-called boezeroen, a kind of shirt usually made of striped cotton. Boezeroenen appear in different regional dresses and have small local differences.

The buttonholes of the Marken boezeroen are finished with black wool thread. The colour of the buttonholes signals the state of mourning: black buttonholes for deep mourning and green for light mourning. Red thread is used when the wearer is not in mourning."
b3792374-f30b-4ff4-b77f-c40e0964b01e.title: Mourning or not?

bbe4ecb8-ecbd-44bc-ac81-a61814beba48.body: "This cap has no regional features. It is ready-to-wear, combined here with regional clothing. The lining of the cap has a stamp from the manufacturer and the seller: the cap was made by the AMKA cap factory in Zutphen and sold by Gerhard Voortman in Rijssen."
bbe4ecb8-ecbd-44bc-ac81-a61814beba48.title: A factory-made cap

f177a501-47cc-46fe-acdb-f064ab52b80d.body: "Take a good look at the clogs. On the instep of these black-painted ones are the letters S.K.G., the owner's initials. When you visited someone on Marken, it was customary to take off your clogs at the door. With your initials on your clogs, you could easily find them again. In many Dutch regional dresses, clogs were a fixed part of weekday clothing. They often had a specific local shape and/or decoration."
f177a501-47cc-46fe-acdb-f064ab52b80d.title: Personalised clogs

0842afa3-da9e-b2d5-0d2e-afa0a2fec615.body:
"In present-day Turkey (since 1923), the bindallı dress is still popular. Through nostalgia for the Ottoman past and the growing visibility of this clothing in Turkish films, television series, politics and education, the bindallı has gained a new cultural meaning.

Today the dress is mainly worn at henna parties. Modern bindallıs vary widely in colour, style and material. Many are machine-made and sold ready-made. Handmade dresses that still use the traditional embroidery techniques do exist, but they are rare and expensive."
0842afa3-da9e-b2d5-0d2e-afa0a2fec615.title: Glittering bindallıs today

1b1780bb-c26c-49ac-a430-e0b0091fd352.body:
"In the late 18th and the 19th century, Ottoman embroidery reached a peak of refinement and quality. New techniques and colours were worked into existing traditions, partly thanks to diplomatic and cultural exchanges between Europe and the Ottoman Empire. Fashion from Paris in particular had a big influence at the time.

The bindallı dress reflects this cross-pollination. Although it can originally be seen as a closed kaftan, bindallıs show clear European influences, such as the length of the dress, putting it on over the head and the low neckline. The style and degree of European influence differed by region and social class, so every dress represents a unique mix of Ottoman and European fashion."
1b1780bb-c26c-49ac-a430-e0b0091fd352.title: Fashion cross-pollination

3fd3adf3-a215-4007-95d1-5a884141950d.body:
