"The technique used, dival, is a thread-laying technique also known as couching. Thin gold threads were wound around a cotton core thread. The design for the motifs on the dress was drawn on various kinds of paper and cardboard. These were cut out with a special knife, ‘stuck’ onto the thick velvet base fabric and fixed in place with the thick thread.

The dival technique took a lot of strength, experience and material, and was done by men in embroidery workshops. Bindalli wedding dresses were therefore expensive."
3fd3adf3-a215-4007-95d1-5a884141950d.title: Cardboard, cotton and gold thread

45ea4092-7f73-437c-bdba-817603035c9e.body: "A wedding dress full of flowers embroidered by hand in gold usually belongs to haute couture. In the 19th-century Ottoman Empire, a dress like this was the fashion for brides. Bindalli literally means ‘a thousand branches’, referring to the embroidered floral motifs on the front and back of the dress. The richly embroidered velvet showed how wealthy you were."
45ea4092-7f73-437c-bdba-817603035c9e.title: A thousand branches

5c77d074-7473-4cf1-9051-75a1cb3520a3.body:
"Floral motifs were everywhere in Ottoman culture: they decorated not only textiles but also pottery, manuscripts and architecture. The flowers were often stylised, with kinds such as tulips, roses, pomegranates and weeping willows freely combined.

In this bindalli wedding dress, too, floral motifs take a prominent place. On the back we see the shape of a vase of flowers, a motif that appeared from the late 18th century onwards.

The flowers are large and placed symmetrically, which gives the dress a stately, almost stiff look. At the same time, the play of overlapping stems, leaves and flowers creates a lively dynamic.”
5c77d074-7473-4cf1-9051-75a1cb3520a3.title: An Ottoman vase of flowers

5d74cb21-a515-4a0e-9b4a-a94185fdf553.body:
"Embroidery was an integral part of daily life in the Ottoman Empire (1299–1922). There was a difference between embroidery made in professional workshops for the court and the embroidery seen in the countryside. At court, wall hangings, banners and kaftans were richly decorated, while in rural life textiles and clothing looked simpler. On festive occasions such as weddings, births and circumcisions, however, beautifully embroidered pieces were shown there too.

A good example of this is the bindallı dress. There were various styles and shapes of bindalli, and wearing one was a form of social and cultural expression. The bindalli dress someone wore gave insight into their socio-economic status: for example through the amount of gold and/or silver thread, the craftsmanship of the embroidery techniques, the complexity of the embroidery patterns, and the European fashion influences visible in the dresses. In short, looking at and studying these dresses helps us understand social continuities and changes in society."
5d74cb21-a515-4a0e-9b4a-a94185fdf553.title: Embroidery as a status symbol

4e24eda5-1e4e-4d77-b7db-65721e14aed8.body: "This flower is made of zinc, a typical material in Lucy Sarneel's work. For her it stood for the everyday and reminded her of the grey-blue Dutch sky and sea. She often made ornaments from it in recognisable shapes such as hearts, curls and flowers, which for her stood for love and protection. Adding these two zinc flowers to her design for this mourning jewellery makes it unmistakably Lucy."
4e24eda5-1e4e-4d77-b7db-65721e14aed8.title: A zinc flower

800594ce-4a69-421a-aec4-c5cbbf28bad0.body:
"This piece of jewellery is about mourning traditions in the traditional dress of Marken. These small triangular panels are removable brooches made of different traditional mourning fabrics. As the mourning lessens, more and more brooches can be taken off, and the colours of the chintz underneath slowly become visible again.

The necklace is a reflection on losing a loved one and, at the same time, on losing traditions. If you turn the necklace further round, you will see what this looks like."
800594ce-4a69-421a-aec4-c5cbbf28bad0.title: Removable brooches for mourning

0b1d02e9-19ee-4cc0-b9f7-6941548cb981.body:
"This almost fantasy-like wide, dark brown wool cloak with a tasselled hood is an akhnif. Typical of these cloaks is the orange-red motif on the back, where a band of patterns is woven across the whole width. These patterns are explained differently in local traditions.

The women who make them call it the eye, which is meant to protect the wearer from evil, especially the evil eye. It is also seen as a mirror, lemri, meant to ward off the feared 'evil eye', or as a half moon, ayyour in Tamazight, the language of the Amazigh, in the dark night. Or as a river flowing straight through the fields. The figure in the middle has also been seen as a snake or lizard. So the pattern has several interpretations, but it is of spiritual importance in any case."
0b1d02e9-19ee-4cc0-b9f7-6941548cb981.title: A protective eye

9b8f757b-6cce-4817-b92c-44d1f32c6573.body:
"The wool cloak is very heavy and feels a little rough because of the goat wool. The coat protects against cold and wind in winter. Amsterdam resident Mohamed Saadouni, who comes from Ait Ouaouzguite, says this about the akhnif":

“I consider the akhnif a very important piece of cultural heritage, because it is a unique and specific garment found only in my home region of Ait Ouaouzguite, and nowhere else in Morocco (or in all of North Africa). I always look at it with great admiration. At home in Amsterdam I have one hanging so I can look at it now and then as a collector's item, and sometimes put it on. As a child I saw them at the carpet market in our village, at the carpet shops and traders. Nobody in my close family wore the cloak, though they did wear other kinds of cloaks or burnouses of wool or cotton, or synthetics, such as the Aznnar, Ahddoen and Aselham. For me personally the motifs don't mean anything specific. They are examples of motifs or symbols used in the region on carpets, clothing, pottery, tattoos and so on. They are generally well-known Amazigh (Berber) signs and motifs that carry and express cultural-historical meaning. They are explained and interpreted differently depending on the region and place. In general they refer to elements and patterns from the natural surroundings, such as animals, water, sun, moon or trees, or to social and cultural traditions and rituals in the region, for example around birth or death.”
9b8f757b-6cce-4817-b92c-44d1f32c6573.title: Experiencing the akhnif in Amsterdam

b40bb998-8fe2-4d3d-9c0b-45276426c7b3.body:
"The akhnif has become an iconic cloak and was therefore often shown in tourist material. Originally it was worn in the mountains, especially by shepherds on long journeys, over a shirt and trousers. It was a typical winter garment worn by both Jewish and Muslim Berbers (Amazigh) from the Aït Ouaouzguite region. The cloaks were almost always made to order . In the first half of the 20th century the akhnif was the most common men's dress in the region, in different sizes for boys too.

With the cloak, people often wore brightly coloured, wool-woven and decorated boots (isjokjad), a turban (rezza) and often a leather shoulder bag (aqqowrab). Jewish men added a black cap and often wore the akhnif inside out.

Tourists loved this garment, which was also a prestige object locally. Today an akhnif easily costs around 300 euros."
b40bb998-8fe2-4d3d-9c0b-45276426c7b3.title: A Moroccan icon

dbb82aca-5c17-46ca-bc57-7189a477c925.body:
"How does this cloak get its unique circular silhouette? The selvage (zelfkant) at the bottom of the garment plays an important role in getting the characteristic semicircular shape. It is made with three extra warp ends. The bottom edge of the cloak has knotted wool fringes, icherbeliyn.

The cloak was woven by hand by women from heavy goat wool in the tapestry weaving technique (tapestry weaving). The decorations are woven in as well.

Want to learn more about how the akhnif is woven? This lecture takes you through the process step by step."
dbb82aca-5c17-46ca-bc57-7189a477c925.title: Women's weaving

f05aa67b-1c5a-4d79-9d7c-850facd385ed.body: "Not much is known about the history of the akhnif and, more generally, of this type of cloak, the burnous, in Amazigh culture. A similar type of burnous in a mixed technique of goat hair and black wool was once worn by shepherds in Sicily (Amahan 1998: 235). This could point to a Roman origin. The Imazighen may have adopted the cappa or toga from the Romans during their occupation of North Africa (148 BC - 4th century). It could certainly also be that the burnous is an Amazigh invention, if we look at the 'burnous shapes' in the prehistoric rock drawings of the Sahara."
f05aa67b-1c5a-4d79-9d7c-850facd385ed.title: Searching for the origin

3e6b24a1-f4f0-42dd-986a-9bf28ff42778.body:
"As you can see, this dress has no sleeves; it hangs from a neck ornament. This original collar is attached to the dress with Velcro. At the end of the 1960s, the designer duo Gijs Bakker and Emmy van Leersum decided that clothing and jewellery should form one whole. The image of this ‘total look’, including hair and make-up, was not to be disturbed, so the models at the 1967 fashion show did not even wear shoes! The focus had to be on the design, which was meant to match the personality of the wearer.

The original dress ended up in the collection of the Kunstmuseum , and the collar in the collection of Design Museum Den Bosch. What you see here is an exact copy of the dress, made, like the original, by Bakker's sister Tiny Leeuwenkamp-Bakker."
3e6b24a1-f4f0-42dd-986a-9bf28ff42778.title: The 'total look'

9d53ee51-e49b-4c7c-bf0b-bb6560b2476b.body: "With this large turquoise collar, Gijs Bakker was one of the first to break away from the traditional forms and materials of goldsmithing, such as elegant silver or gold chains. To keep his large jewellery from being too heavy and too expensive, and in protest against jewellery as a status symbol, he used a light and cheap material: aluminium. Through anodising, a popular technique in the 1960s, he could change the colour of the aluminium. This process changes the structure of the outer layer, so the added colour becomes a hard-wearing part of the metal."
9d53ee51-e49b-4c7c-bf0b-bb6560b2476b.title: Coloured metal

aacbc4f9-1fad-4d10-a344-f1e3e89a01e3.body:
"This collar is unlike any other because it is one piece of metal from which half circles have been sawn. It is wide and rigid, while most necklaces are thin and flexible. The designer Gijs Bakker ignores the traditional language of forms: as a fundamentalist, he makes rational designs.

He also believes jewellery should not be a separate addition but part of the wearer. That is why this design follows the shapes of the body, with room for the shoulders and the head. Wearability was not the priority, though, because it is hard to get over your head."
aacbc4f9-1fad-4d10-a344-f1e3e89a01e3.title: Unlike any other

c2243459-3e66-4261-bef9-bbc90699220e.body: "The streamlined shapes, the cool blue colour and the shine of the aluminium collar and the silk dress create a futuristic look that fits well with the ‘Space Age’. In the 1960s, space travel was a source of inspiration for the fashion world, because it was developing fast after Sputnik had been launched and the first human had been to space. When this collar dress was presented in 1967, otherworldly music could be heard from the album ‘Fantasy in Orbit. Round the World with Electronic Music’ by Tom Dissevelt."
c2243459-3e66-4261-bef9-bbc90699220e.title: Fashionable shapes for the Space Age

09119173-ce3f-4da3-a6a8-2ebcd5cbf267.body:
"Can you see the extra fabric hanging around the knee here? It is not there for decoration but for a practical reason. In the riding habit the wearer could ride elegantly: with both legs on one side, as was proper for a lady at the time.

Riding was then exclusively an elite sport. Riding side-saddle required special riding clothes made to measure. This skirt from the collection is long and has an extra insert at knee height to fit over the saddle, because the legs had to stay completely covered. After dismounting, the long skirt was lifted a little and buttoned up with a loop at the waist or elsewhere on the skirt so the rider could walk in it.”
09119173-ce3f-4da3-a6a8-2ebcd5cbf267.title: Riding side-saddle

1bca53a5-3090-4fb7-bb37-0430d29d6afd.body:
“This is not just any costume, but one for riding. Sport and travel became more and more popular at the end of the nineteenth century. Women too could take up all kinds of sports, such as riding, swimming, tennis, hockey and korfball, but also rowing, skating and cycling. Despite the many health benefits of sport, which were by then widely known, it also brought new problems:

“Madam Etiquette has one great enemy, and that is sport, for however hard the former may try to keep people confined in the garment of convention, sport tears this garment to shreds, wraps itself in a roomy, comfortable, practical robe, and.... leaves convention for what it is.’’ 

To be able to move ‘decently’, special sports costumes were designed for ladies, which could be bought or made to measure at department stores, respectable fashion houses or dressmakers. Sportswear still followed the fashionable silhouette , in which ladies had to wear a skirt, as with this riding habit.”
1bca53a5-3090-4fb7-bb37-0430d29d6afd.title: Adapted sport for women

1e9c5979-b154-4a99-8609-e33e3df16360.body:
"Clothing was a precious possession. Gowns and suits that went out of fashion were not thrown away but remade or carefully kept. Sometimes a garment held special memories. This robe à l’anglaise, for instance, is said to have been worn by Wilhelmina van der Putten (1743-1810) at her wedding to Cornelis Maas (1741-1811) on 23 February 1766.

The gown was later donated to the museum by the heirs of Johanna Houkjen Staring-Blussé, Wilhelmina's great-granddaughter, in whose family the dress had been used as a dressing-up gown. At her grandparents' golden wedding in 1890, Winanda Arnoldina Staring (1876-1945) wore the gown. She made a fine couple with Piet Blussé, also in eighteenth-century costume."
1e9c5979-b154-4a99-8609-e33e3df16360.title: Marrying, dressing up, keeping

8964a4b3-4141-4b3e-99d2-fd46938cbca3.body:
"Old gowns were regularly brought out for dressing-up parties. In the nineteenth century, dressing up was a popular pastime, in all levels of society and not only at carnival but all year round. Associations such as skating clubs and dance schools organised fancy-dress parties for ‘ordinary’ people. Well-to-do citizens amused themselves at masked balls and costume parties at court and in clubs. At private parties at home, guests liked to entertain each other with tableaux vivants: ‘living paintings’ showing important events from national or family history, but also allegories and myths.

The historical costumes still lying in the attic came in handy then. This silver-blue gown of Wilhelmina's was also brought out several times for special occasions. In 1928 Coralie Vriesendorp (1912-1972) was photographed in the gown. In this way the memory of a great-great-great-great-grandmother stayed alive and tangible, and the gown brought a lot of fun at dressing-up parties."
8964a4b3-4141-4b3e-99d2-fd46938cbca3.title: 162 years later: posing in costume

013a317a-28d1-43f5-a3e8-ff2485d1c50d.body: "Parachutes during the war were first made of silk. When Japan occupied Asia's silk-producing regions, the Allies switched to nylon, a new synthetic fibre from DuPont. In the Netherlands, nylon was still a rare and expensive novelty. This smooth, light "parachute silk" was often really nylon, as this gown is. Parachute “silk” made for a very durable material that often resisted creases as well and thus made for excellent upcycling material."
013a317a-28d1-43f5-a3e8-ff2485d1c50d.title: Why a parachute?

5662a38b-a9a9-48b8-9d36-67e7e2ebf096.body: "This christening gown was once a parachute. Mrs. 't Jong made it in 1947, when it was still hard to find new fabric in the Netherlands after the second world war. Look for the diagonal seam across the skirt: it was sewn onto the original parachute and not by her. The names and christening dates of the babies who wore the gown are embroidered along it, hiding the line. The slightly uneven shape of the overall dress tells the same story: the gown was cut from cloth not meant for clothing."
5662a38b-a9a9-48b8-9d36-67e7e2ebf096.title: Making something new out of something old

6cf11c2a-5af2-4cd2-9f81-9d369c340b4f.body: "Seventeen names are stitched on this gown marking a baptism. The first belongs to Mrs. 't Jong's eldest child, christened in 1947. Over the following decades, sixteen more of her children and grandchildren wore it, the last in 2013. Every time, a new name and date was embroidered by hand. The name of the local vicar, the church, and the Bible text read at the service is also embroidered on the gown. Few garments keep such a precise record of the ones who wore them as this one after the second world war."
6cf11c2a-5af2-4cd2-9f81-9d369c340b4f.title: Seventeen embroiderd names

110d49a1-4230-408e-aa32-4e2d648f5d2d.body:
"On the back of the cap, this floral damask motif will appear and disappear as the light hits the fabric. Although black in appearance, this hat is full of small decorative details that only come out in certain lights and when seen up close - like the moiré effect of the ribbons or these damask motifs.

Damask is a fabric in which the reversible motifs are directly woven in. It is often (but not always) made on a jacquard loom, and the pattern is created by a contrast of binding systems. Damask motifs often only appears as the fabric moves or the light changes."
110d49a1-4230-408e-aa32-4e2d648f5d2d.title: Light-sensitive motifs

d4121e4b-e0a2-4f72-80e7-e85a56e97066.body:
"These “rabbit-like” ears are in fact very unusual to German regional wear.  This type of black ribbons that form the “ears” are present in other regions’ traditional headwear but rarely formed into stiff bows like these ones. People are often more familiar with the Bollenhut - a hat with pompoms- when thinking of the Black Forest.

It seems like these black-bow bonnets might have been more commonly worn by (married) women of smaller means, than the ones who chose the alternative of an “ear-less” and gold- embroidered one. These “ears” really allow to identify the wearer, where they come from and their place in society."
d4121e4b-e0a2-4f72-80e7-e85a56e97066.title: Rabbit-like ears

f2d2edca-75df-4a69-a58d-8f0217abdbe2.body:
"If you peek through the tulle veil, you will find a colourful surprise hidden underneath.

Flowers are everywhere on this cap, in very discreet ways - such as on the damask motifs on the cap or the tulle edge of the veil - but also in the colourful inner lining of the hat. The lining is in bright green with white and pink flowers. It is quite touching to imagine that this rather extravagant detail (in contrast to the black of the exterior) of the hat would only be known to its wearer; it’s a secret bouquet of flowers."
f2d2edca-75df-4a69-a58d-8f0217abdbe2.title: A colourful surprise

1f82494e-9730-4a28-b51e-e5bd944b47af.body:
"The sortie is richly decorated with different techniques and materials. This one is from the early 20th century, and thanks to the labels inside we know it was made by the fashion house Maison de Paris on the Plaats in The Hague.

This sortie has the shape of an enlarged collar. The finely pleated satin duchesse creates a very rich effect, made even richer by alternating with gold lace and couched gold thread. The short double stand-up collar is of white silk voile; the strips of voile at the bottom edge are combined with fine machine-made lace. The most striking feature of this sortie is the long streamers hanging from two rosettes."
1f82494e-9730-4a28-b51e-e5bd944b47af.title: Maison de Paris: luxury made in the Netherlands

d57a9937-87cc-4a5e-903b-a775f9cc2833.body:
"The short evening cape, or sortie (‘sortir’ is French for ‘to go out’), was worn over evening dress when gala dress was required. On such occasions the queen and the ladies of the court wore a white dress with a train, a low neckline and short sleeves. Long white gloves up to the upper arm were also a required part of gala dress .

So the sortie did not have to be very long. It did have to meet a few requirements: it had to be comfortable on the way to a gala event at the palace. Outside the palace walls it had to offer protection against rain, wind, draughts and cold. It had to be made of light material so as not to crush the gala dress and corsage, and with its richness it was certainly allowed to stand out when getting in and out of the carriage or court car. Thanks to this photo, we know that Queen Wilhelmina wore this sortie during her visit to Artis (Amsterdam's zoo)."
d57a9937-87cc-4a5e-903b-a775f9cc2833.title: Covered up and dressed up for Artis

0594a8bd-9474-4f07-9cc0-1e830766c118.body:
"Take a good look at the material: here silk chiffon has been tufted into jute. A special combination.

Jan Taminiau had approached the TextielLab's tufting department to make fabrics for his new couture collection. A rather unusual request, because it usually makes heavy tufted wall hangings and rugs, not refined, supple fashion fabrics. Taminiau, however, managed to make this carpet technique work for him.

It was soon decided not to work with the usual material, wool, because it would be too heavy. After some tests with ribbons in different fabrics, strips of silk chiffon turned out to be the most suitable: this material gives a lot of volume without becoming heavy. Strips of green silk and a gold-coloured knitted ribbon were used as well."
0594a8bd-9474-4f07-9cc0-1e830766c118.title: Tufting with silk chiffon

d8aee340-7955-4ac4-8600-2a4fbfaa8fcd.body:
"Turn the object around and be surprised!

According to Jan Taminiau, the common thread in the collection is wrapping and unwrapping yourself, looking for the right shape for the moment. The cocktail dresses from the 'Follies' collection can be changed into a completely different silhouette in no time.

With this dress, the arms can be put through the front of the skirt and the skirt can then be draped over the shoulders: the dress has turned into a stole."
d8aee340-7955-4ac4-8600-2a4fbfaa8fcd.title: Wrapping and unwrapping

f0c10f53-4ad7-4628-8e64-1994bb736beb.body: "Normally, rubber latex is applied to the back of a tufted rug to fix the tufted material in place. But this makes the rug stiff, so it would not work for a skirt or dress whose fabric has to ‘fall’. That is why Taminiau sewed all those strips of tufted silk to the jute by hand."
f0c10f53-4ad7-4628-8e64-1994bb736beb.title: Painstaking work

f3418307-b484-4657-af53-386c15bfc16f.body:
"Normally the TextielLab tufts onto a base of grey polyester that cannot be dyed. That colour was not an option for Taminiau. Jute, the material later used to finish the back of the rugs, did suit him in colour. It is also a material Taminiau often works with, like his famous jute mailbag.

However, it is not possible to tuft directly onto jute. As a solution, Taminiau suggested embroidering the jute onto a polyester canvas and tufting through both layers, and that worked. Afterwards he had the grey polyester canvas pulled out by hand in his studio, thread by thread. When the dress is worn as a stole, the jute is nicely visible in the parts that are not tufted."
f3418307-b484-4657-af53-386c15bfc16f.title: A jute base

4fba6be7-0835-4e28-b7b0-13df933e31c3.body:
"You can't see it from the outside, but the collar of this black wool jacket is badly worn on the inside from use. To prevent further damage, the whole collar was protected with a layer of tulle during restoration. I dyed the tulle a matching neutral brown so that it almost disappears against the fabric. The reinforcement is only visible when you zoom in on the detail photo of the inside.

The jacket itself is made of wool tibet and decorated with sewn-on embroidered appliqués. The lining is striped cotton, a common combination at the time."
4fba6be7-0835-4e28-b7b0-13df933e31c3.title: Hidden wear

66c4e95d-788b-4676-b6ca-ad773ad4e6c9.body:
"This simple pelerine of wool tibet, lined with calendered brown cotton twill, shows clear signs of use. You can see this from the few fringes that are missing, and the sewn-on velvet ribbon is worn in several places. This is especially visible at the buttons: the covering of the wooden buttons has worn away completely in some places.

Also note the fine hand-set stitches with which the whole lining has been carefully attached, as seen in the photo above."
66c4e95d-788b-4676-b6ca-ad773ad4e6c9.title: A well-worn pelerine

7072973a-d865-9988-7468-b4cd9f16ae28.body:
"Although cashmere was known in Europe as early as the 17th century, it became a fixed part of fashion at the beginning of the 18th century. In the late 18th and early 19th century, ladies wore Empire gowns that hardly kept them warm.

Cashmere shawls were the answer for keeping the body warm. They also had an impressive function: because of the exclusivity of cashmere at first, the shawls became a status symbol, the fashionable textile of the well-to-do middle class.

In 1805 Joseph Jacquard designed a machine that could produce cashmere shawls in large numbers, known as the Jacquard loom. The machine was soon used in the textile mills of the Scottish town of Paisley, where producers focused mainly on the great demand for cashmere shawls and started making copies on a large scale.

That is how an imitation cashmere shawl like this one ended up on the shoulders of a woman in Brabant."
7072973a-d865-9988-7468-b4cd9f16ae28.title: The shawl as an it-item

7c572fe5-9442-ae24-5948-3fe83a93f99e.body:
"In this photo from around 1895 we see Helena van der Zanden and her husband Koos van Dongen. They were photographed in their everyday clothes in front of their home in Bavel (Breda). 

Koos came from a working-class family and worked, among other things, as a farmhand. Johanna ran the household, cared for their five children and probably also helped on the land where she could. 

Helena wears a black outfit similar to the one shown here, her everyday clothes, and that is unusual: people usually had their photo taken in their best clothes. She wears black, not because she was in mourning, but because around 1900 it was fashionable in Brabant regional dress."
7c572fe5-9442-ae24-5948-3fe83a93f99e.title: How it was worn: a personal story

7c6bebb2-5dbd-8b67-9c22-b3cfe5acbe31.body:
"As always happens in fashion with luxury “it” items, they also have to become available to the masses. The shawl we see here is a good example. It is less supple and soft than a real cashmere shawl and was woven in Europe. 

In the late 19th century it was a fixed part of Brabant regional dress. In everyday speech it was also called a palmdoek (palm cloth) or worteldoek (root cloth). When the shawls went out of fashion in the countryside too, they were not thrown away: they were used as tablecloths or as an eye-catcher on the wall."
7c6bebb2-5dbd-8b67-9c22-b3cfe5acbe31.title: From wrap to home textile

f788c9d5-c33d-40bd-bd62-9880f4ddd06f.body:
"You have to look for it, but here you see one of the few examples of extra decoration on the West Brabant everyday cap. Along the first strip, small pins have been stuck in that make the cap sparkle.

This simple and cheap way of decorating with pins is typical of the people of the poor Brabant countryside. Because, as people in Brabant say: 'the sun also likes to shine through small windows.'"
f788c9d5-c33d-40bd-bd62-9880f4ddd06f.title: Pin cap
